docs.title: Writes, transactions, drivers
docs.text: Feature PostgreSQL SQLite / MySQL Notes RETURNING yes (Returning: true) MySQL: no; MariaDB: INSERT ... RETURNING only (InsertReturning) .Returning(cols...), .ReturningAll() on insert, update, delete; read with .Rows(ctx). Identity read-back in CreateGraph needs it. INSERT ... SELECT yes: Insert[T].FromSelect with SelectExprs (FROM-less or one source, with Where) or Select[T] as the source; composes with OnConflict, Returning, Upsert[T] SQLite yes (WHERE true is added to a SelectExprs or Select[T] source with FROM and no WHERE before ON CONFLICT); MySQL plain insert only (no ON CONFLICT; FROM-less with WHERE renders FROM DUAL) Target columns are explicit typed columns of T; a select-list count mismatch is ErrValidation. No model hooks, automatic timestamps, Go-side defaults or validators are applied: list those columns yourself. The soft-delete filter on a SelectExprs source needs a TableRef that carries the soft-delete marker. Upsert / ON CONFLICT yes (OnConflict: true) MySQL and MariaDB: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE through the same calls, with the conflict target limited to the only unique key of the table (otherwise ErrUnsupported); see mysql.md Upsert[T] (target = primary key) or Insert[T].OnConflict(cols...).DoNothing() / .DoUpdate(assigns...) with SetExcluded. Upsert neither advances nor checks the version column. OnConflict(...).Where(preds) (partial-index target) and .DoUpdate(...).Where(preds) (conditional update, col.Excluded()): PostgreSQL yes; SQLite: bool, integer, finite float and string values in the target predicate render inline so they match the index text (golden-tested, not yet run against a real SQLite; momo.SQL("live = 1") is the proven fallback; the values show up in logs and traces; write index literals as Momo renders them, integers as 2 and floats in plain decimal with .0 for whole numbers for magnitudes from 1e-6 up to 1e21 and exponent form (1e-07, 1e+21) outside that range, otherwise use momo.SQL), any other value or Excluded() there is ErrValidation; MySQL ErrUnsupported. Graph writes yes SQLite: yes, covered by the integration tests that run on SQLite; MySQL: not covered by a MySQL integration test yet CreateGraph, FindOrCreate (needs ON CONFLICT), UpsertByPK Merge, BulkUpdate, Truncate yes: Merge is PostgreSQL 15 or later and .Returning needs 17 or later (ErrUnsupported on an older server or a driver without ServerVersioner); BulkUpdate updates only the listed keys (PostgreSQL); Truncate is TRUNCATE TABLE Merge and BulkUpdate: ErrUnsupported. Truncate: SQLite runs DELETE FROM and resets the autoincrement counter; MySQL runs TRUNCATE TABLE (refused inside a transaction) Merge returns ErrValidation when an interceptor adds predicates (deny the kind instead). Truncate runs interceptors with the kind truncate, has no RESTART IDENTITY or CASCADE, and is refused inside a MySQL transaction. Merge does not run field validators on the inserted values Bulk COPY yes: Insert[T].Copy (after Omit, with the models as its argument) on the pgx driver; also momo.CopierOf(querier) for the driver call SQLite and MySQL: Copy returns ErrUnsupported (neither sqlitedriver nor mysqldriver has a Copier) Copy runs the insert interceptors (deny only) and BeforeInsert over a copy of the models; it skips OnConflict, Returning and chunking, and it counts as a write for NewUnitOfWork. On a *DB with WithImplicitTx it runs in its own transaction; on a pinned handle with WithTxSetup it fails closed. Not available through FromSQLDB Batch (several statements, one round trip) driver level: momo.BatcherOf(querier); relation loading uses it automatically SQLite: no (sqlitedriver has no Batcher); MySQL: no (mysqldriver has no Batcher) not available through FromSQLDB Transactions yes: db.Tx(ctx, opts, fn), db.Begin; read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable; read-only SQLite and MySQL: commit, rollback and panic cases run in the shared suite (suite.RunAll); SQLite accepts the default and serializable isolation only (other levels ErrUnsupported) and runs read-only transactions through PRAGMA query_only (sqlitedriver tests) any other sql.IsolationLevel: ErrUnsupported (Op "begin") Savepoints yes: Tx.Savepoint, RollbackTo, Release SQLite and MySQL: yes, covered by the shared suite (suite.RunAll) a dialect without savepoints: ErrUnsupported (Op "savepoint") Pinned connection yes: db.OnConn(pc) SQLite and MySQL: the drivers implement Pinner (driver tests); db.OnConn itself is exercised by a MySQL test (generated keys) and not by a SQLite test no transactions on a pinned *DB: Begin, Tx, Replace and CreateGraph fail with ErrUnsupported (Op "begin"), chunked Insert with Op "insert"; Link, Unlink and Count work SET col = DEFAULT, VALUES (DEFAULT) yes SQLite: no DEFAULT in VALUES a multi-row insert that is default in some rows only fails with ErrUnsupported where the dialect cannot express it

docs.title: Secrets in errors, hooks and connections
docs.text:
• Argument masking: with WithArgLogging, a value bound from a column tagged sensitive reaches hooks as momo.RedactedArg, not the value. This covers insert values, Set and SetExpr assignments on insert, update and upsert (every argument inside an expression assigned to a sensitive column), the primary-key and version predicates of a model update or delete, keyset After values, and WHERE predicates in which a sensitive column is one operand: the comparison methods, EqExpr and the other expression comparisons, In, NotIn, Between, Like, ILike, ContainsLiteral, ArrayContains, ArrayContainedBy, ArrayOverlaps, AnyOf, and the same methods on an expression that reads a sensitive column such as Lower of it. Relation loading, Link, Unlink, Replace and Count mask key values bound to sensitive key columns, including join-table columns that map to them. The database still receives the real value. QueryEvent.Args is always a copy, so a hook cannot replace or reorder the bound arguments. The copy is deep for []byte and json.RawMessage values only, so changing those in place does not reach the driver; other mutable argument types are shared. Known gaps: arguments passed to raw momo.SQL or momo.TypedSQL fragments are not masked, because Momo cannot tell which column they belong to; SQLite renders values in an ON CONFLICT target predicate as SQL literals, so such a value appears in QueryEvent.SQL. Do not enable argument logging where raw fragments or conflict-target predicates carry secrets. Error.Detail() is also unmasked: it returns the raw driver detail, which for a PostgreSQL constraint violation quotes the offending key values, including sensitive ones. Do not log it or return it to clients; Error() is the safe text.
  • Encode errors: the pgx driver withholds the text of pgx client-side encode failures, which quote the bound value, on every path (pool, transactions, pinned and adopted connections, the database/sql adapter, rows). The message keeps the argument position, such as args[2]; the original error stays reachable with errors.Is, errors.As and Unwrap. That unwrapped cause still contains the bound value, so code that logs every link of an error chain must not print the causes.
  • Simple protocol: pgxdriver.WithExecMode, FromConnConfig and FromSQLDB refuse simple protocol, which interpolates values client-side, with ErrUnsupported. FromConnConfig checks the config it is given. FromSQLDB cannot read the pgx config of an opaque *sql.DB, so it checks the first connection it uses, on the first statement, not at construction. Only that first connection is checked: a custom connector that varies the exec mode per connection is not checked.

docs.title: Multi-tenant row-level security
docs.text:
Row-level security (RLS) policies usually read a setting such as current_setting('app.tenant_id', true). The fail-closed pattern sets that setting at the start of every transaction from a scope carried in the context.Context, so a statement that forgot its scope matches no rows. WithTxSetup and WithImplicitTx build that into the *DB:

db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool),
    momo.WithTxSetup(func(ctx context.Context, tx *momo.Tx) error {
        id, ok := tenantFrom(ctx)
        if !ok {
            return nil // no scope: nothing is set, the policy matches no rows
        }
        return momo.SetConfigLocal(ctx, tx, "app.tenant_id", id)
    }),
    momo.WithImplicitTx(),
)

ALTER TABLE documents ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE documents FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON documents
  USING (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::bigint)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = nullif(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::bigint);

Connect as a role without BYPASSRLS that does not own the tables (or use FORCE, as above): superusers and BYPASSRLS roles skip every policy.

Feature Behavior WithTxSetup The function runs right after every transaction momo begins: DB.Begin, DB.Tx, and the transactions momo opens itself (chunked inserts, graph creation, relation writes, WithSearch, implicit transactions). It runs once per real transaction, not per savepoint, and not for AdoptTx (the caller began that transaction). An error rolls back and is returned. WithImplicitTx Auto-commit statements on a *DB (Select, Insert, Update, Delete, Exec, Scalars, relation loads) each run in a short transaction, so the setup applies. Iter, Each and Rows hold the transaction until exhausted or closed, then commit; a scan or driver error rolls back, and so does a cancelled context for a write or a read abandoned early (a fully drained read still commits). Close early-abandoned rows to free the connection. SetConfigLocal set_config(key, value, true): the setting ends with the transaction. The same as Tx.SetLocal. Not used on an implicit *DB Pipelined relation loading (Batch) and the raw driver COPY path, because they bypass the setup (Insert[T].Copy instead runs in its own transaction). BatcherOf and CopierOf report none for such a *DB; use a Tx for them.

A behaviour change for WithImplicitTx on an unpinned *DB only: the rows of an Insert, Update or Delete with RETURNING (Rows) must be read to the end before Close. A write closed unread, or after reading only the first row (for example UpdateQuery.Rows or DeleteQuery.Rows users who read one row and close), is rolled back and Close returns ErrValidation; this includes a panic that unwinds through the loop. Handles without WithImplicitTx, a Tx and a pinned OnConn handle are unaffected, and FindOrCreate, UpsertByPK and CreateGraph read to the end themselves.

Without WithImplicitTx, auto-commit statements on a *DB run outside any transaction, so the setup never applies to them and they are unscoped. Use WithImplicitTx (or DB.Tx) whenever the setup enforces a security boundary. Statements run through db.Driver() bypass momo and its hooks entirely, so they are never scoped either.

The setup does not cover everything. AdoptTx transactions are the caller's, so apply the setting yourself. momo migrate and Go migrations run outside the *DB options, so they are never scoped; run them as a role that may bypass the policies. A handle from OnConn cannot begin a transaction, so on a *DB configured with WithTxSetup its statements fail with ErrUnsupported instead of running unscoped, and it reports no COPY or Batch path. A panic in a setup function rolls the transaction back before it propagates, and a panic in an Each or Iter callback rolls back the implicit transaction. If the context is cancelled before a streaming implicit write is closed, the write is rolled back and Close and Err return the context error.

Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode use only transaction-local settings (SetConfigLocal), never a session-level SET: the session belongs to whichever client PgBouncer hands the backend to next. TestImplicitTxPgBouncer runs concurrent tenants through PgBouncer and checks no scope leaks.

docs.title: PgBouncer and TLS
docs.text: Feature PostgreSQL Notes PgBouncer, transaction pooling yes, with the default exec mode The default pgx.QueryExecModeExec sends unnamed statements and binds server-side. TestPgBouncerNoNamedPreparedStatements checks on the wire that no named prepared statement is created. WithExecMode also accepts CacheStatement, CacheDescribe, DescribeExec; the simple protocol is rejected with ErrUnsupported. Do not run momo migrate through a transaction pooler. A search_path set at connection start does not reliably survive pooling; SearchSettings and Tx.SetLocal use transaction-local set_config, which does. TLS yes, as configured by the pgx connection string (sslmode, sslrootcert, ...) NewPool(ctx, url) hands the URL to pgx. Momo adds no TLS options. momo migrate prints a TLS warning when the URL has sslmode=disable and a non-loopback host. Use sslmode=verify-full for remote databases.

  • make test-compilefail: compile-fail tests for the typed API

Every test that needs a database lives in a file that starts with the //go:build integration tag, next to the SPDX line, and gets its database from internal/testdb or testopen. make test, and the macOS and Windows CI jobs, build without the tag and so run unit tests only; they cannot skip a database test silently because they never compile one. make test-integration sets MOMO_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1, so an unset database URL fails the run. docs.title: Full-text search
docs.text: PostgreSQL full-text search has a column type and typed expressions in Momo. Every builder here returns ErrUnsupported when the statement is built for SQLite or MySQL.

docs.title: The column
docs.text:
A model field of type types.TSVector maps to a tsvector column (and a types.TSQuery field to tsquery). Both are codecs, so the generator and migrate pick the column type from the Go type, diff it and read it back from the database with no drift. The Go value is the text form PostgreSQL prints, for example 'cat':3 'fat':2. A nullable column is a *types.TSVector.

The application normally never sets this column (leave it nil on insert and update: the trigger overwrites it). Keep it current with a trigger declared in MomoConfig, and index it with GIN:

type Article struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:kb_articles"`
    ID         int64            `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Title      string
    Body       string
    SearchTsv  *types.TSVector
    Embedding  vector.Vector `momo:"dim:1536"`
}

func (a *Article) MomoConfig(c *momo.Config) {
    c.Index("kb_articles_search_gin", &a.SearchTsv).Method("gin")
    c.Function(schema.Function{
        Name: "kb_articles_tsv", Returns: "trigger", Language: "plpgsql", Volatility: "VOLATILE",
        Body: "BEGIN NEW.search_tsv := setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(NEW.title, '')), 'A') || " +
            "to_tsvector('english', coalesce(NEW.body, '')); RETURN NEW; END;",
    })
    c.Trigger(schema.Trigger{
        Table: "kb_articles", Name: "kb_articles_tsv_trg", Timing: "BEFORE",
        Events: []string{"INSERT", "UPDATE"}, ForEachRow: true, Function: "kb_articles_tsv()",
    })
}

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
The text search configuration (english, simple, ...) is a string. It is bound as a parameter and cast to regconfig, so it cannot carry SQL; an empty one fails the build with ErrValidation.

Builder SQL Result type momo.TSMatch vec @@ query Predicate momo.ToTSVector to_tsvector(config, text) TSExpr[types.TSVector] momo.WebsearchToTSQuery websearch_to_tsquery(config, text) TSExpr[types.TSQuery] momo.PlainToTSQuery plainto_tsquery(config, text) TSExpr[types.TSQuery] momo.PhraseToTSQuery phraseto_tsquery(config, text) TSExpr[types.TSQuery] momo.ToTSQuery to_tsquery(config, text) TSExpr[types.TSQuery] momo.TSRank ts_rank(vec, query [, normalization]) TSExpr[float64] momo.TSRankCD ts_rank_cd(vec, query [, normalization]) TSExpr[float64] momo.TSHeadline ts_headline(config, text, query [, options]) TSExpr[string]

The query text, the configuration and the headline options are always bound parameters. The normalization argument of the rank functions is the optional PostgreSQL flag mask (0 to 63) and renders as a literal. WebsearchToTSQuery accepts any user input without raising a syntax error, so it is the builder for a search box; ToTSQuery expects tsquery syntax and a malformed query is a database error.

A TSExpr has As, Asc, Desc and the comparison methods of any scalar expression, so it works in Where, OrderBy and Columns:

q := momo.WebsearchToTSQuery("english", userInput)
rank := momo.TSRankCD(articleSearch, q)

hits, err := momo.Select[Hit](db).
    From(momo.TableRef{Name: "kb_articles"}).
    Columns(articleID, rank.As("rank"),
        momo.TSHeadline("english", articleBody, q, "StartSel=<b>, StopSel=</b>, MaxFragments=2")).
    Where(momo.TSMatch(articleSearch, q)).
    OrderBy(rank.Desc()).
    Limit(20).
    All(ctx)

Here articleSearch is a Column[types.TSVector] and articleBody a Column[string]. Without a stored column, search a text column directly with momo.ToTSVector over articleBody as the first operand of TSMatch (an expression index on the same expression keeps it fast).

Every use of a call binds its own parameters (the configuration and the query text), so the same expression written in the select list and again in GROUP BY gets different placeholders, and PostgreSQL rejects the statement as an ungrouped column. The same applies to SELECT DISTINCT with an ORDER BY on the call. Group by a stored tsvector instead, or compute the call once in a subquery or CTE and refer to its alias. A golden test pins the placeholders.

Arguments bound by these calls are masked in hook events (shown as RedactedArg) when an operand reads a column marked sensitive; the driver still receives the real values.

docs.title: Hybrid ranking: vector plus text
docs.text:
Momo has no built-in fusion step (reciprocal rank fusion is not built). Combine the two signals in one score with the typed arithmetic helpers. The cosine distance is lower for better matches and the text rank is higher, so subtract a weighted rank from the distance and order ascending:

dist := momo.CosineDistance(articleEmb, queryEmbedding) // vector.Vector
text := momo.TSRankCD(articleSearch, momo.WebsearchToTSQuery("english", userInput))
score := momo.SubExpr[float64](dist, momo.Mul[float64](text, 0.5))

hits, err := momo.Select[Hit](db).
    From(momo.TableRef{Name: "kb_articles"}).
    Columns(articleID, score.As("score"), articleTitle).
    OrderBy(score.Asc()).
    Limit(20).
    All(ctx)

This scores every row. To restrict the candidate set to text matches, add a Where on TSMatch over articleSearch and the same query, which lets the GIN index prune the rows before the vector distance is computed. The TestFullTextHybridRanking integration test runs this pattern.

docs.title: Scanning
docs.text: pgx returns tsvector and tsquery values as text, which types.TSVector and types.TSQuery scan. ts_rank and ts_rank_cd return real; they scan into float64 fields.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes you from an empty module to a program that talks to PostgreSQL through Momo. It stays small on purpose: the first program uses no generated code. The full loop (models, momo generate, migrations, typed queries, relations, vector search) is the quickstart example, which is compiled and run end to end in CI.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Go 1.26 or newer.
  • PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension installed on the server. The momo migrate command and the full vector support are PostgreSQL only. SQLite (cgo driver, with vectors through sqlite-vec; the pure-Go driver has no vectors) and MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7 and MariaDB 11.8 run queries and writes, and have library migration dialects (migrate/sqlite, migrate/mysql) but no CLI support (see capabilities).
  • A role that may create extensions, or a superuser who runs CREATE EXTENSION vector once in the target database. The first generated migration creates the extension when a model has a vector column.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Add the library to your module and install the CLI at the same version:

go get github.com/azrtydxb/momo@latest
go install github.com/azrtydxb/momo/cmd/momo@latest

Pin an explicit version instead of latest in a real project, and keep the CLI and the library on the same one. The supported Go and PostgreSQL versions are listed in supported versions.

docs.title: Connect and run SQL
docs.text:
pgxdriver.NewPool opens a pgx pool, pgxdriver.New wraps it as a Momo driver and momo.New returns the *momo.DB. db.Tx runs a function in a transaction and commits when it returns nil. Inside it, use the tx handle for every statement. momo.Exec and momo.Scalars are the raw SQL path: ? binds the next argument, so values never become part of the SQL text.

The program reads the connection string from MOMO_EXAMPLE_DSN, for example postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/scratch?sslmode=disable. It creates a temporary table inside the transaction, so it leaves nothing behind.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "os"

    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
)

func main() {
    if err := run(context.Background()); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func run(ctx context.Context) error {
    pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("MOMO_EXAMPLE_DSN"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer pool.Close()
    db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

    return db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {
        if _, err := momo.Exec(ctx, tx, "CREATE TEMP TABLE notes (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, body text NOT NULL)"); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if _, err := momo.Exec(ctx, tx, "INSERT INTO notes (id, body) VALUES (?, ?)", 1, "hello"); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        bodies, err := momo.Scalars[string](ctx, tx, "SELECT body FROM notes WHERE id = ?", 1)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Println(bodies)
        return nil
    })
}

docs.title: Handle errors
docs.text:
Momo classifies database errors into sentinels. Compare with errors.Is, never with error text. This program violates a primary key on purpose and branches on momo.ErrUniqueViolation; the transaction rolls back when the function returns the error, so the table disappears with it.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "os"

    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
    "github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("MOMO_EXAMPLE_DSN"))
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer pool.Close()
    db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

    err = db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {
        if _, err := momo.Exec(ctx, tx, "CREATE TEMP TABLE tags (name text PRIMARY KEY)"); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        for range 2 {
            if _, err := momo.Exec(ctx, tx, "INSERT INTO tags (name) VALUES (?)", "go"); err != nil {
                return err
            }
        }
        return nil
    })
    if !errors.Is(err, momo.ErrUniqueViolation) {
        log.Fatalf("want a unique violation, got %v", err)
    }
    fmt.Println("duplicate rejected")
}

Every Go block in these docs is checked in CI: a block is either a complete package main program that must compile, a program marked as runnable (this one runs against PostgreSQL on every build), or an explicitly marked fragment that must still parse as Go.

docs.title: Typed queries
docs.text:
Typed queries need generated code. You describe a table as a struct that embeds momo.Model, run momo generate, and build queries from the generated descriptors, so a misspelled column or a wrong value type fails at compile time:

momo generate
momo migrate diff init
momo migrate apply

The quickstart example shows the models, the momo.yaml configuration, the generated packages and the first migration. Then read:

  • Agent guide: the complete reference in one file, from tags to errors, with the pitfalls.
  • Type mapping: the column type for each Go type.
  • Migrations: what momo migrate does and how to recover.
  • Relations, projections and vector search.

docs.title: Importing models from other ORMs
docs.text:
Momo can read the models of an existing GORM, Bun or Ent project and write the equivalent Momo structs. Three packages do the reading:

Package Reads importer/gorm GORM structs and their gorm:"..." tags, gorm.Model importer/bun Bun structs and their bun:"..." tags importer/ent the Ent schema package (fields, edges, indexes, mixins)

Each package exports one function, Read(dir string), that returns the neutral []importer.Model and an *importer.Report. importer.Emit turns the models into Momo source through the generator's writer.

The readers are static. They parse the Go files of dir with go/parser and never compile, load or execute your code, so reading a project cannot run its init functions, hooks or migrations. The flip side is that they see only what is written as a literal in those files: a naming strategy set in another package, or an index added by a migration, is not visible. Each reader's package comment lists its limits.

The momo import command is not wired yet (story 228). Today the readers are a Go API: call Read, check the report, then Emit.

docs.title: The import report
docs.text:
A Momo model is never an exact copy of an ORM model, because the ORMs differ in behaviour you do not see in the struct: GORM replaces a zero value with the column default, Ent saves an edge only when its setter was called, and so on. The importer does not paper over these differences. Every one becomes a Change in the report, with the source position (file:line:col), the model, the field and a message. Report.String() prints one line per change, sorted by position, in the form source: kind: Model.Field: message.

Read the report before you trust the converted models. Report.Has(kind) and Report.Of(kind) filter it in code. The kinds are:

Kind Meaning zero-value-handling the source ORM treats a zero value as unset and applies a default; Momo writes the zero value (use a pointer to leave it unset) implicit-save the source ORM saves an association together with its parent; Momo writes only the model you pass go-default the source ORM computes a default in Go (timestamps, generated values); Momo needs a tag or a database default unsupported something the reader cannot convert (an unreadable tag, an unknown builder call, a type with no mapping); convert it by hand renamed-type the field type changes on import, for example gorm.DeletedAt becomes *time.Time, and the automatic filter does not carry over dropped-field a field that does not become a column (ignored with -, scan-only, relation fields) is not imported dropped-index an index Momo's tags cannot express (a composite index, a second index tag on a field) is not imported; declare it in the companion file naming a table, column, constraint or foreign key name that Momo derives itself, or a naming strategy the reader cannot see; check the names version-mapped a migration version was renumbered while importing migration history (importer/history) go-side-rule a validator, immutable field, hook or policy that the source ORM runs in Go and Momo does not

The importer never drops one of these silently: an empty report means the reader found nothing to flag, not that it checked behaviour it cannot see.

docs.title: Migration safety and recovery
docs.text:
Momo v0.3.0, PostgreSQL (SQLite and MySQL as libraries, sections 3a and 9). Every statement here was checked against migrate/, cmd/momo/, schema/ and dialect/; the tests that pin a behavior are named. For the first run see README, Create and apply the migration.

momo migrate runs PostgreSQL only; with another dialect it exits 2 ("migrations for dialect ... are not available yet"). SQLite has a migration dialect for use as a library, described in section 3a, and MySQL and MariaDB have one described in section 9.

docs.title: 1. Model
docs.text:
models (Go structs) --momo migrate diff--> <v>_<name>.up.sql + <v>_<name>.snapshot.json + momo.sum
                                              |
database <--------momo migrate apply---------+  (history table: momo_migrations)

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
All files live in one directory per dialect (default migrations/postgres, set migrate.dir.postgres or --dir). diff writes exactly three files:

File Content <version>_<name>.up.sql Statements. Header -- momo:generated, plus -- momo:destructive and/or -- momo:no-transaction when needed. Statements are separated by a blank line and each ends in ;. <version>_<name>.snapshot.json The whole schema after this migration, wrapped as {format_version, version, parent, schema}. schema carries its own format_version. momo.sum Checksum manifest of every file in the directory, rewritten by diff.
  • version is a 14-digit UTC timestamp (YYYYMMDDHHMMSS). If the clock is not past the latest existing version, diff uses the second after it, so versions only grow.
  • name must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$.
  • .down.sql files are optional and hand-written (diff never generates one). They are hashed in momo.sum, and apply never runs them. Only Engine.Rollback runs them (section 2).
  • Files whose name starts with . are ignored everywhere (.DS_Store, .momo-*.tmp). A symlink to a directory inside the migration directory is an error. Moving an applied file into a subdirectory is fine: history is keyed by version, not path (TestMovingAppliedMigrationIntoArchiveKeepsHistory).
  • diff never overwrites a file (exit 1 if one exists) and writes all-or-none: temporaries first, then publish, momo.sum last.

docs.title: Format versions
docs.text:
Artifact Field v0.3.0 value Newer than this binary Snapshot wrapper format_version 1 read error, "upgrade momo" Embedded schema schema.format_version 1 read error, "upgrade momo" momo.sum header # momo.sum format=N 1 read error History table checksum of the row __momo_meta__ 1 apply refuses, "upgrade momo"

A snapshot without format_version is rejected.

docs.title: Diff
docs.text:
momo migrate diff <name> runs offline (no database, no driver). It loads the models, compares them with the snapshot of the highest version in the directory (the empty schema when there is none), orders the changes by dependency and renders SQL. No difference: prints no changes, exit 0, writes nothing.

  • Renames are never guessed. A drop plus an add prints a hint: possible rename ...; pass --rename-table old=new or --rename-column table.old=new.
  • Dropped extensions and schemas are not dropped in the database; diff prints a hint that they are no longer managed.
  • Diff never reads the database. A table that is already populated is indistinguishable from an empty one (see section 5).

diff does not depend on momo generate. momo generate --check verifies only the generated *_gen.go files (exit 1 and stale: <path> lines when stale). There is no momo migrate diff --check. To fail CI when the models have no migration, run momo migrate diff ci_probe on a clean checkout and fail unless it prints no changes (when there is a difference it writes files and exits 0, so also check git status --porcelain on the migration directory). This recipe is derived from the code, not covered by a test.

docs.title: Checksums
docs.text:
Two independent checks, both SHA-256 of the file bytes:

  1. momo.sum must match the directory: every file present, none added, removed or changed. Apply, Status and Baseline refuse otherwise (ErrChecksumMismatch, naming the files). A missing momo.sum is an error that names momo migrate hash. momo.sum itself carries a directory hash; a hand-edited momo.sum is rejected.
  2. The history row of an applied migration stores the checksum of its up file. Apply refuses when that file changed since (the error says ... changed after version V was applied).

Plan and Drift do not check either.

docs.title: History table
docs.text:
momo_migrations. Every statement against it (read, insert, update, delete and the CREATE TABLE) names the table schema-qualified and quoted, for example "app"."momo_migrations". The table is resolved before the lock is taken, and again right after, and the advisory-lock key is built from that resolved schema, so a migration that changes search_path cannot redirect the history writes. If the two lookups disagree (another process created the table in an earlier schema in between), the lock is released and the attempt is repeated once; a second disagreement fails with an error asking you to retry.

  • An existing table is found the way earlier versions found it, through the session search_path, and its schema is then used. Installs made with the unqualified name keep working, and no second table is created.
  • The resolved object must be a regular, permanent table, and the connecting role must be its owner or hold the privileges of the owning role (pg_has_role with USAGE, so a role with NOINHERIT does not qualify). A superuser holds every role's privileges, so a superuser migrator additionally requires the owner to be itself or another superuser; a table owned by an ordinary role is refused, because its triggers and rules would run with superuser rights. A view, foreign table, unlogged or temporary table, or a table owned by an unrelated role, named momo_migrations earlier on the search_path, is refused with a validation error naming the schema, the table and the owner; it is never used. A table adopted on first install by CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS passes the same checks after the statement runs.
  • What this does and does not defend: it stops a foreign-owned or non-table object that sits ahead of the real table on the search_path from capturing the history writes. It does not stop a role whose privileges you hold, or another superuser, from owning such an object, and it cannot protect a schema that other roles may write to and that is ahead of yours on the search_path before any table exists. Keep schemas on the migrator's search_path writable only by the migrator.
  • With no table yet, it is created in the current schema. Config.Schemas[0] (migrate.schemas) must equal the current schema (current_schema) or the engine returns a configuration error naming both. plan, status and drift on a connection with no current schema and no table report an empty history; apply and the other writers fail.
  • momo does not SET search_path for the migration session. Migrations are written against the search_path of the connection you give momo and may rely on it; qualify the history table, not the migrations. Set the search_path in the connection URL, and pin it per role with ALTER ROLE on the migrator role.
Column Type Meaning version TEXT PRIMARY KEY Migration version name TEXT Migration name checksum TEXT SHA-256 of the up file status TEXT running, applied, failed, rolled_back (and meta) statements_applied INTEGER Statements that completed error TEXT Failure text, empty on success applied_at TEXT RFC 3339 UTC execution_ms BIGINT Duration apply_id TEXT UTC timestamp plus 8 hex digits, shared by one apply run; baseline for baselined rows kind TEXT sql

One extra row, version = '__momo_meta__', status = 'meta', holds the history format version. ReadHistory and Inspect hide it and the table. running and failed are "dirty". rolled_back is not dirty.

docs.title: How apply decides what to run
docs.text:
1. Take the migration lock, set session timeouts, create the history table if missing.
  2. Refuse (ErrDirty, exit 3) if any row is running or failed.
  3. Refuse (ErrChecksumMismatch, exit 3) on a checksum problem (above).
  4. Pending = every *.up.sql and every registered Go migration (section 6a) whose version has no row other than rolled_back, run in ascending version order, optionally stopping after --to N (a version without a file is refused, so a typo applies nothing).

The test is "has no row", not "is newer than the latest applied". An older file that appears later (a merged branch) is still applied, after newer ones. apply does not check snapshot parents; validate does (section 2).

docs.title: Drift
docs.text:
momo migrate drift inspects the live database and compares it with the snapshot of the latest applied migration (the empty schema if none, so every object is unmanaged). Exit 0 and no drift, or exit 1 and one line per finding:

Line Meaning changed: <kind> <name>: <detail> In both, definition differs. A column, index or constraint present only live is changed: ... not in snapshot on that object. An invalid index is changed: ... invalid index (failed CONCURRENTLY build). missing: <kind> <name> In the snapshot, not in the database. unmanaged: <kind> <name> In the database, not in the snapshot: tables, views, functions, enums, schemas, extensions (every extension except plpgsql, for example pg_stat_statements, pgcrypto), and triggers/policies on managed tables. unverified: <kind> <name> Not compared and does not affect the exit code (below).
  • Extension versions are ignored when either side leaves the version empty.
  • Hide objects you do not manage with migrate.exclude (globs over name or schema.name; they apply to tables, views, functions, enums, extensions, triggers and policies). Example: exclude: ["pg_stat_statements", "audit_*"].
  • momo_migrations is never reported.
  • A view query, trigger WHEN and policy USING/WITH CHECK changed outside migrations is not detected; those objects are listed as unverified: only. Exit 0 does not prove their text matches. Function bodies are compared.
  • Declared text (defaults, checks, index predicates) is canonicalized through a scratch schema in a rolled-back transaction, which needs CREATE on the database. Without it drift still runs but can show false changed entries (never hides a real one).

docs.title: 2. CLI
docs.text:
momo has three commands: generate, migrate, help. Global exit codes: 0 success, 1 findings, 2 usage/config, 3 database/lock/execution (migrate).

Shared flags on every migrate subcommand: --config/-c momo.yaml, --dir, --dialect, --url.

Command Needs DB Does Exit 1 when diff <name> [--rename-table a=b]... [--rename-column t.a=b]... [--allow-destructive] [--stage] [--enforce-not-null] no Write a migration (section 1, 5). destructive or staged refusal; target file exists; model diagnostics plan yes List pending migrations with statement counts. Read-only, no lock, creates nothing. never apply [--to N] [--lock-wait 30s] yes Apply pending. a chain refusal (ErrBranchConflict, ErrChainInvalid, ErrOutOfOrder); other failures are 3 status yes One line per version: applied, pending, dirty, mismatch, missing. Read-only. any version not applied/pending validate [--db] no (--db yes) Directory checks (below); --db adds status. any problem or unhealthy status hash no Recompute momo.sum, list files it accepts as changed:/added:/removed:, write it. never new --custom <name> no Write an empty hand-written migration (section 6). a file would be overwritten baseline --version N [--force] yes Record migrations through N as applied without running them (section 7). database differs from snapshot drift yes Section 1. any change, missing or unmanaged resolve --version N --applied or --rolled-back yes Settle a dirty migration (section 4). never rehash --version N [--accept] yes Show, and with --accept store, the new checksum of an edited applied migration (section 4). without --accept, when the file differs

validate checks: files parse and directives are known; momo.sum matches; versions unique and increasing; each snapshot's parent exists; no two snapshots share a parent (branch conflict); each up file has a snapshot; a hand-written migration (no -- momo:generated) has a snapshot equal to its parent's. Use it in CI. apply runs the chain checks too (fork, missing parent, cycle, gap) and refuses with the same message (a fork is ErrBranchConflict; a missing parent, cycle or gap is ErrChainInvalid; both exit 1, like validate findings), and it refuses with ErrOutOfOrder (exit 1) when a pending version is older than the latest applied one, so a late-merged older migration is never applied after newer ones (TestApplyRefusesForkedChain, TestApplyRefusesPendingOlderThanApplied, TestApplyRefusesBrokenChain, TestMigrateChainRefusalsExitOne).

Recovering from ErrBranchConflict or ErrOutOfOrder (there is no rebase command yet). Both mean two teammates branched from the same snapshot and both merged: two snapshots share a parent, and one of the new migrations has a version older than the other. Fix it in the files of the branch that merged last, before it is applied anywhere. The late migration is still pending, so it needs no rehash:

  1. Delete its <version>_<name>.up.sql and <version>_<name>.snapshot.json (a generated migration; for a hand-written one rename the .up.sql to a version later than the newest applied one and copy the newest snapshot to the same new version, with parent set to the previous snapshot).
  2. Run momo migrate diff <name>. It compares the models with the latest snapshot and writes the migration again with a new version and the right parent.
  3. Run momo migrate hash, review the changed:/added:/removed: list, and run momo migrate validate.

If the older migration was already applied somewhere, do not rewrite it: leave the chain as it is and add a new migration for the difference.

momo migrate new --custom <name> writes an empty hand-written migration (section 6). Not wired into the CLI yet (story 098): rebase, lint, rollback. Each exits 2 with migrate <name> is not available yet. The engine already has two of them, for Go callers:

  • Engine.Rollback(ctx, RollbackOptions{Group: false}) runs the .down.sql of the last applied migration (the applied row with the greatest applied_at); with Group: true it runs the downs of every row that shares the greatest apply_id, in descending version order. It takes the same lock and session timeouts as Apply, refuses a dirty database or a checksum mismatch, and returns ErrNoDown before running anything when any selected version has no down file. A transactional down runs in one transaction together with the history update; the row becomes rolled_back, so the version is pending again and the next apply runs it anew. A down with -- momo:no-transaction runs statement by statement and, if one fails, leaves the row failed (dirty, settle it with resolve). A rollback undoes schema, not data: write the down so that it can run on a populated table (TestRollbackGroup, TestRollbackNoDown).
  • Engine.Rebase(ctx, target, desired, name) takes the directory of the target branch (from git, Momo has no git dependency). It lists every file of the branch's migrations that the target lacks, refuses with the file name when one has no -- momo:generated header, and regenerates one migration on top of the target's latest snapshot. It first validates the target (momo.sum, chain, snapshots) and refuses a broken one, and it refuses a branch migration that has a hand-written .down.sql, naming the file. It writes nothing: the caller deletes the returned files and writes the new ones (TestMigrateRebase).

There is no --force-unlock: the PostgreSQL lock is a session advisory lock that the server frees when its holder's connection ends (section 3). --lock-wait exists on apply only. --lock-wait 0s fails immediately when locked. resolve and baseline wait the default 30 s.

Database URL: --url, else the variable named in migrate.url_env.postgres, else MOMO_DATABASE_URL. Prefer the environment, or --url -, which reads the URL from standard input (printf '%s' "$URL" | momo migrate apply --url -): a --url value shows in the process list of a shared host, and momo prints a warning on stderr when it sees one.

momo.yaml migrate: keys: dir, url_env (maps keyed by dialect), schemas, lock_timeout, statement_timeout (Go durations), exclude, external_extensions (section 7).

docs.title: 3. Apply semantics on PostgreSQL
docs.text: One connection is pinned for the whole run. Order: lock, set timeouts, history table, migrations, reset timeouts, unlock (reset runs first so a small statement_timeout cannot cancel the unlock). Cleanup runs on a context detached from Ctrl-C and has two steps: the two RESETs share one 5 s bound, and the unlock has its own.

docs.title: Lock
docs.text:
pg_try_advisory_lock(id) on the pinned session, polled every 200 ms until --lock-wait (default 30 s) passes. id = FNV-64a of momo:<schema>.momo_migrations, where <schema> is the schema of the resolved history table (the current schema when none exists yet), so schemas are independent. On timeout apply exits 3 with migration lock is held by another process: held by pid=N application_name=X (TestApplyLockWaitTimesOutWithHolder; waiting callers proceed once it is released, TestApplyWaitsForLockRelease).

The lock is session-scoped: it is released when the holder's connection ends, so a crashed process frees it. There is no lock row to delete and no flag to force the lock (--force-unlock was removed: it never did anything). If a lock appears stuck, find the session (pg_stat_activity by the pid in the message) and terminate it with pg_terminate_backend.

apply, resolve and baseline take the lock. plan, status, drift, validate do not.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
• Default: one transaction per migration file, not per batch. The running history row, all statements and the update to applied commit together. A second migration failing never undoes a first that committed.
  • Marked -- momo:no-transaction: the whole file runs with no transaction, one autocommitted statement at a time, with statements_applied updated after each. Every statement in that file loses atomicity, not only the concurrent one. Only the directive selects this mode on apply; apply does not inspect statements. diff writes the directive when it renders a concurrent index. A hand-written file must carry the directive itself: otherwise PostgreSQL rejects CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction, the version is recorded rolled_back, and it can be retried after you add the directive. diff never mixes the two modes in one file: when a diff holds both transactional DDL and statements that must run outside a transaction, it writes two migrations, the transactional one first and a trailing <name>_no_tx one that carries the directive (one second later version). A failure in the first file rolls it back whole. A diff with only such statements writes the single no-transaction file.
  • Statements run one by one with no bind parameters. The splitter respects strings, comments and $$ bodies; -- momo:split disables dollar-quote awareness and splits at every semicolon.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY applies correctly when it is in a no-transaction file: the index is valid and the version is applied (TestCreateIndexConcurrentlyApply). diff produces it from Concurrently() on a model index, and for ADD UNIQUE and the VALIDATE CONSTRAINT of an ADD CHECK (section 5).

docs.title: Session timeouts
docs.text:
Applied with SET on the pinned session, RESET at the end:

Setting momo.yaml Default Notes lock_timeout migrate.lock_timeout 5 s A DDL statement that cannot get its table lock within the limit fails with SQLSTATE 55P03; the transaction rolls back and the version stays retryable. Key absent: 5 s. 0s sets lock_timeout = 0, which disables the limit. statement_timeout migrate.statement_timeout not set Left as the role or server default. A role-level statement_timeout therefore applies to long migrations such as index builds. Use a migration role without it. Key absent: untouched. 0s sends SET statement_timeout = 0, which disables the limit even when the role has one (for a long index build).

If RESET fails, the connection is discarded rather than returned to the pool.

docs.title: PgBouncer and other poolers
docs.text: Run migrations on a direct connection or a session-pooled one. Under transaction pooling the advisory lock, the SET lock_timeout and the search_path belong to a server connection that the next statement may not reuse, so the lock does not protect and the timeouts can leak or not apply. The driver's default query mode is PgBouncer-safe for application queries; the migration engine through PgBouncer is not tested in v0.3.0. A startup search_path is also not reliable through a pooler, so set the schema on the role or on a direct connection.

docs.title: 3a. SQLite
docs.text:
migrate/sqlite is the SQLite migration dialect. It is a library API: pass it to the engine with migrate.WithDialect(sqlite.New()) and a driver/sqlitedriver driver (cgo, not Windows). The momo migrate command does not select it yet, so there is no --dialect sqlite. The tests that pin the behavior below run on a real SQLite in the integration suite (TestSQLiteInspectRoundTrip, TestSQLiteAlterDecision, TestSQLiteRebuild, TestSQLiteLockTable, TestSQLiteEngineLifecycle, TestSQLiteRenderApplyInspectDiffIsZero).

Inspection. Tables, columns (type, NOT NULL, default, collation, generated expression), the primary key, UNIQUE constraints, indexes (including expression and partial indexes), foreign keys, CHECK constraints, views and triggers. The momo_migrations and momo_migration_lock tables, the sqlite_ tables, virtual tables and the shadow tables of virtual tables are left out. An INTEGER PRIMARY KEY of a rowid table is reported with identity by_default, and the schema normalizer gives that column the same identity on the model side, so the two compare equal. A trigger is its CREATE TRIGGER text (Trigger.Definition), compared after whitespace and case outside quotes are normalized. Extensions, native enums, functions, policies, partitions, row-level security and schemas do not exist on SQLite and are never reported.

Enums. SQLite has no enum type. A TEXT column that carries CHECK ("col" IN ('a', 'b')) is inspected as an enum column whose enum is named <table>_<column>, and Engine.Diff writes an enum column back as that CHECK. A model enum therefore round-trips without a diff only when it is named <table>_<column>. create_enum and drop_enum produce no statement; alter_enum_add_value rebuilds the tables that use the enum.

ALTER or rebuild. SQLite changes a table in place only for these: ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO, RENAME COLUMN, ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN, and index, view and trigger statements. The renderer uses them when the restrictions in the SQLite documentation allow it: an added column must not be PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, a stored generated column, an enum or identity column, or NOT NULL without a non-NULL default, and its default must not be CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (or CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIME) or a parenthesised expression; a dropped column must not be in the primary key, a UNIQUE constraint, an index (key or WHERE), a CHECK, a foreign key (either side), a generated column's expression, a trigger or a view. Everything else (alter_column, any primary key, unique, check or foreign key change, and an add or drop of a column that breaks a restriction) rebuilds the table, and all changes to that table in the same diff become one rebuild.

The rebuild follows the 12 steps in the SQLite documentation. diff writes them as plain statements into the up file and puts -- momo:sqlite-foreign-keys-off at the top of the file. On apply the engine runs PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF outside the transaction (the pragma does nothing inside one), runs the file in one transaction and turns enforcement back on afterwards, also when the migration failed. The statements are: drop every view and trigger that mentions the table (directly or through another view), CREATE TABLE "new_<table>", INSERT ... SELECT of the columns the old and new table share, DROP TABLE, RENAME, CREATE INDEX for each index, recreate the dropped views and triggers that the desired schema keeps unchanged, and PRAGMA foreign_key_check. If that pragma returns a row the statement fails with momo.ErrForeignKeyViolation naming the table and row, and the transaction rolls back (TestSQLiteRebuildOrphanRollsBack). Row count and content, indexes, triggers and views survive (TestSQLiteRebuild, TestSQLiteRebuildKeepsDataAndObjects) and foreign keys are enforced again afterwards (TestSQLiteRebuildFKStillEnforced).

Limits of the rebuild:

  • After each recreated view the file runs SELECT 1 FROM "view" LIMIT 0, because CREATE VIEW does not check the names in its query. A view that names a dropped column therefore fails the migration. sqlite.Rebuild with migrate.RunStatements reports that as migrate.ErrRebuildBlocked naming the view; a migration read back from a file has lost the statement hints, so the engine reports the failing statement number instead.
  • A trigger body is resolved only when the trigger fires, so a trigger that names a dropped column is recreated and fails later.
  • A table can be rebuilt only if it has columns in common with the new definition; INSERT is skipped otherwise.
  • sqlite.Rebuild and sqlite.Capture rebuild from a live connection (captured views and triggers are recreated verbatim); the engine path rebuilds from the snapshot instead.
  • A model cannot declare WITHOUT ROWID, STRICT or AUTOINCREMENT, so a table that has one in the database and not in the model is not a difference: diff and AutoMigrate leave it alone and a rebuild writes it back (TestSQLiteAutoMigrateWithStrictTable). Asking for one the table lacks is refused by diff (write a custom migration). schema.Table carries Strict and Autoincrement; inspection reads them. A rebuild of an AUTOINCREMENT table copies its sqlite_sequence value to the new table, so ids of deleted rows are not handed out again (TestSQLiteStrictAutoincrementRoundTrip). An INTEGER PRIMARY KEY DESC is not a rowid alias and is not reported as an identity.
  • A down migration that rebuilds a table carries the same -- momo:sqlite-foreign-keys-off line; Rollback honours it as apply does (TestSQLiteRollbackRebuildKeepsChildRows).

Unsupported. These fail with an error that wraps momo.ErrUnsupported instead of being dropped: create_schema, create_extension, the policy and row-level-security changes, the function changes, materialized views, views with indexes, index storage parameters, an access method other than b-tree, operator classes, NULLS FIRST/LAST in an index, column comments, serial identity, identity on anything but an INTEGER primary key, partitioning.

Lock. A row in momo_migration_lock (id = 1, holder, acquired_at), created on first use. A second holder gets ErrLocked with held by pid=N host=H at=T; apply polls it like the PostgreSQL lock until --lock-wait. Unlock deletes the row only while it still carries this holder's text. A process that dies leaves the row behind: after checking that nothing is migrating, call sqlite.ForceUnlock(ctx, conn), which returns the holder it removed (there is no CLI flag). The lock and statement timeouts of the session options do nothing on SQLite; busy handling is the driver's busy_timeout.

Other differences. DDL is transactional, so one migration is one transaction. AutoMigrate skips any change to an existing table that needs a rebuild (an enum column, say) with the reason "requires a table rebuild; use a migration", because a rebuild writes the whole desired table and would also apply the changes AutoMigrate leaves alone (TestSQLiteAutoMigrateSkipsRebuilds). Index parts carry no collation in the schema, so a collation on an index key is not compared. Collation on a column is.

docs.title: 4. Failure and recovery
docs.text: Check state with momo migrate status (exit 1 when anything is dirty, mismatched or missing). Read error, shown after the colon.

docs.title: Transactional migration fails (TestPostgresApplyRecovery)
docs.text: DDL and the history row roll back; nothing the file did persists. A rolled_back row records the error. That is not dirty: status shows pending <v> <name>: <error>, and the next apply retries from statement 1. Fix the cause (or fix the file, section "editing", then momo migrate hash) and run apply again. Data-exception errors (SQLSTATE class 22) store only the code, not the message, because the message may quote data.

docs.title: Interrupted (Ctrl-C, killed, lost connection)
docs.text:
• Transactional: the server aborts the transaction; no running row survives. Same as above. After a Ctrl-C, rollback and the failure row are still written (5 s bound).
  • No-transaction: the running row was committed, so the version stays dirty (running or failed). The lock is released when the connection dies.

docs.title: No-transaction migration fails (partial state)
docs.text:
Statements before the failing one are committed. The row is failed, with statements_applied = n and the error. Every later apply stops with ErrDirty (TestApplyRefusesDirtyAndReleasesLock) until you resolve it.

  1. momo migrate status, note the version and statements_applied.
  2. Inspect the database. Statement n+1 is the one that failed.
  3. Make the database match one of two states by hand with psql:
  4. finish the file yourself, then momo migrate resolve --version V --applied (the row becomes applied, error cleared, checksum of the file as it was when the run started is kept); or
  5. undo the committed statements, then momo migrate resolve --version V --rolled-back (the row is deleted; the version is pending again and will run from statement 1). A file may be edited before the next apply: the version has no applied row, so edit, momo migrate hash, apply.
  6. resolve takes the migration lock and errors when the version has no running or failed row.

docs.title: A down migration fails (Engine.Rollback)
docs.text:
A transactional down that fails rolls back with its history update: the schema is unchanged and the row stays applied, so the database is not dirty (TestRollbackTransactionalFailureLeavesRowApplied). Fix the down and run Rollback again; if you edit the file, run momo migrate hash first.

A down with -- momo:no-transaction commits statement by statement. When one fails the row becomes failed with statements_applied = n and an error that starts with down:, and every later apply or Rollback stops with ErrDirty (TestRollbackNoTxFailureLeavesRowFailed). Both resolve states are valid; choose by what the database looks like after you repair it:

  • resolve applied (ResolveApplied): the migration is still in effect. Use it when the failed down changed nothing that matters or you undid its partial work. The row becomes applied, the error is cleared, and the version can be rolled back again (TestResolveAppliedAfterFailedDown).
  • resolve rolled_back (ResolveRolledBack): the migration is gone. Use it when you finished the down by hand. The row is deleted, the version is pending, and the next apply runs the up file again (TestResolveRolledBackAfterFailedDown).

Rollback verifies momo.sum first, down files included: an edited or added .down.sql is refused with ErrChecksumMismatch naming the file even when the matching up file is no longer in the directory (TestRollbackChecksumMismatch). It takes the migration lock like apply (TestRollbackTakesTheLock).

docs.title: Invalid index after a failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
docs.text:
PostgreSQL leaves the index in place, marked invalid, when the build fails (for example a uniqueness violation or a cancelled build). Momo does not use IF NOT EXISTS, so re-running fails with "already exists" until you drop it.

  1. momo migrate drift shows changed: index <table>.<name>: invalid index (failed CONCURRENTLY build).
  2. DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS <schema>.<name>; in psql.
  3. Fix the data or definition.
  4. momo migrate resolve --version V --rolled-back (if the row is failed), then momo migrate apply. If the failing file contained other statements, handle them per the previous subsection first.

baseline also counts an invalid index as a mismatch.

docs.title: Editing an already-applied migration
docs.text:
apply and status refuse (checksum mismatch, naming the file; status shows mismatch). momo migrate hash does not fix this. It rewrites momo.sum, but the history row still holds the old checksum, so apply still refuses. Options:

  • Revert the file (git checkout -- <file>), then write a new migration for the change. This is the supported path.
  • If the edit is cosmetic (whitespace or a comment) and you accept it: run momo migrate hash (momo.sum), then momo migrate rehash --version V to see the recorded and the new checksum, then momo migrate rehash --version V --accept to store it. Without --accept nothing changes and the command exits 1 and says so. With it, only the row of version V is updated, and the row's error column records checksum accepted by rehash at <time>: <old> -> <new>, which status shows. The edit is accepted, not run: the database is not changed, so rehash only edits that do not alter what the migration did (TestRehash, TestRehashOnPostgres, TestMigrateRehashAcceptsEditedMigration).

Editing a migration that is not applied yet (status pending) is fine: run momo migrate hash to accept it. hash records whatever is on disk, so review the printed changed:/added:/removed: list first.

A history row whose file is gone shows missing and exit 1 on status.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: apply with nothing pending prints no pending migrations, exits 0, and runs no migration. It takes the lock (an advisory lock, not a write) but writes nothing: it does not create the history table or its meta row, so it works with a read-mostly role. When something is pending, the history table is created first (TestApplyNothingPendingWritesNothing, TestApplyNothingPendingCreatesNoHistoryTable). Running it twice, or two processes at once, is safe: the second waits for the lock, then finds nothing to do (TestConcurrentApply, TestConcurrentApplyWaits). plan, status, drift are read-only.

docs.title: 5. Production safety checklist
docs.text: What Momo enforces, what it only hints at, what it does not see. A complete worked upgrade (add column, index, rename) is examples/upgrade-database.

docs.title: Refused unless you opt in (diff, exit 1)
docs.text:
--allow-destructive is required for: drop_table, drop_column, drop_enum, and a column type change (alter_column with a different type). The file then carries -- momo:destructive. Review these. Type changes render as ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING col::type: a full table rewrite under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which fails on rows that do not cast.

Not destructive, but reported as risky: hints by diff (no flag needed): dropping an index, primary key, unique, check or foreign key; adding a unique or check constraint (both can fail on existing data).

  • ADD CHECK is written NOT VALID; its VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (a full scan that does not block writes) goes in the trailing no-transaction migration. If the validation fails, the trailing migration is failed and apply stops with ErrDirty. The constraint stays NOT VALID: it still checks new rows. Recovery: fix the offending rows, run ALTER TABLE t VALIDATE CONSTRAINT c; in psql, then momo migrate resolve --version V --applied (V is the _no_tx version). resolve --version V --rolled-back runs the whole file again from its first statement, so it is safe only when the file holds just the failed VALIDATE. If earlier statements of the file (a CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, another VALIDATE) already committed, they would fail with "already exists": use --applied after finishing by hand, or undo those statements first (see "No-transaction migration fails").
  • ADD UNIQUE on an existing table is CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY followed by ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX, both in the trailing no-transaction migration. On duplicate rows the build fails and leaves an INVALID index (drift reports it): drop it with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS, fix the data, then resolve --rolled-back and re-apply (the unique index is the first statement of its file; if other statements of that file already committed, undo them first).
  • On a partitioned table (including a sub-partitioned one) ADD UNIQUE is a plain, transactional ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE, and an index declared with Concurrently() is created and dropped without CONCURRENTLY, because PostgreSQL rejects CONCURRENTLY there. ADD CHECK keeps the NOT VALID form (TestPartitionedTableConstraintsAndIndexes).
  • diff leaves out the explicit drop of an index, unique, foreign key or primary key that lists a column dropped in the same diff: DROP COLUMN removes it, and an explicit drop after it would fail. A check or an index expression or WHERE that merely mentions a dropped column's name anywhere in its text cannot be classified reliably, so its drop is written DROP ... IF EXISTS, which is correct whether or not the column took it.
  • Limit: an inline foreign key in a new CREATE TABLE cannot reference a unique constraint that the same diff adds to another table, because that unique is created in the later no-transaction migration and the foreign key would fail. Workaround: run diff twice, first the unique on the existing table, then the new table with its foreign key.
  • Not flagged at all: dropping a view, function, trigger or policy, and any change you write by hand.

The -- momo:destructive header is informational. diff writes it and --allow-destructive is the only guard, and that guard exists in diff only: apply does not read the header or scan statements, so a hand-written file with a DROP applies without confirmation. Review every .up.sql in code review.

docs.title: NOT NULL columns
docs.text:
An added NOT NULL column (or an existing column made NOT NULL) with no default, identity or generation expression is refused (ErrStagedRequired) for any table that already exists in the snapshot. diff never queries the database, so it cannot tell whether the table has rows: an empty existing table is refused too. A column that looks like a rename (same table and type as a dropped column) is refused the same way; the message names --rename-column. With --stage, then --enforce-not-null:

  1. diff --stage adds the column as nullable and prints the hint staged: T.C was added as nullable; backfill it, then run migrate diff with --enforce-not-null to emit ALTER TABLE T ALTER COLUMN C SET NOT NULL. The new snapshot records the column as nullable, like the database will have it, so validate and status agree after you apply.
  2. Apply, backfill in batches outside the migration.
  3. Check the backfill: SELECT count(*) FROM T WHERE C IS NULL must return 0.
  4. diff <name> --enforce-not-null emits ALTER TABLE T ALTER COLUMN C SET NOT NULL and records NOT NULL in the snapshot. A plain diff (without the flag) is still refused, because only you know the backfill is done. Apply it. The statement scans the table under a lock; do it when the table is quiet or add a validated CHECK first by hand.

Several columns can be staged in separate migrations before any backfill: each stays recorded as nullable until enforced, and one --enforce-not-null emits SET NOT NULL for all of them. The flag enforces every column that is nullable in the snapshot and NOT NULL without a default in the model, not only staged ones, so backfill all of them first. New NOT NULL columns stay refused.

If NULLs remain, apply of the SET NOT NULL migration fails (exit 3). The migration is transactional, so it rolls back: the version is rolled_back (not dirty), status shows it as pending with the error, and nothing changed. Finish the backfill and run apply again. Only a hand-edited -- momo:no-transaction file can leave a dirty row; settle that with momo migrate resolve --version V --applied or --rolled-back (section 4).

The same applies to an existing column made NOT NULL: diff --stage writes nothing (the snapshot already has the column nullable; the hint is only printed when the same run writes other changes), and diff <name> --enforce-not-null emits the SET NOT NULL after the backfill. --enforce-not-null only affects existing columns: a new NOT NULL column without a default still needs --stage.

A NOT NULL column with a default is not staged. A constant default is cheap on PostgreSQL 11 and later. A volatile default (random(), clock_timestamp(), gen_random_uuid(), nextval(...) and a few more well-known functions) rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; diff prints a risk: hint (PostgreSQL only) for an ADD COLUMN with one on an existing table. It only knows the built-in names it lists; a function you wrote yourself is not checked.

docs.title: Other items
docs.text:
• Backfills: Momo has no data-migration step. Do them in a hand-written migration (section 6) or a separate job. A long backfill inside a transactional migration holds its locks until commit and can hit lock_timeout/statement_timeout.
  • Large-table indexes: declare Concurrently() on the index in MomoConfig. diff then writes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own no-transaction migration, so the build does not block writes. Without Concurrently() the index is a plain CREATE INDEX that blocks writes while it builds. Set a role without statement_timeout for the run. A hand-written alternative: examples/custom-sql-migration.
  • Lock timeout: the default 5 s lock wait fails fast instead of queuing behind a long transaction. A retry is safe for transactional migrations.
  • Deploy order: migrate first, then roll out code, with every migration backward compatible with the running code (add before use; drop only after no code reads it; rename as add, copy, switch, drop).
  • Run once: one apply job per deploy. Concurrent applies are safe but wait up to --lock-wait.
  • Backups: take a backup or snapshot before any destructive, type-change or no-transaction migration. PostgreSQL DDL rolls back only inside a transaction; no-transaction files cannot be rolled back.
  • CI: run momo generate --check, momo migrate validate, and the model-vs-migrations probe from section 1 on every change.
  • After: momo migrate status (exit 0) and momo migrate drift.
  • Roles: CREATE EXTENSION (pgvector, and any extension the models declare) needs a role allowed to create it. A missing package or privilege is reported, with exit 3, as extension "x" is not installed (install its server package and run CREATE EXTENSION as a role that may). If a superuser creates the extension by hand, list it in migrate.external_extensions so no migration emits it (section 7).

docs.title: 6. Custom SQL migrations
docs.text:
Worked example: examples/custom-sql-migration.

momo migrate new --custom <name> (offline) writes the three files for an empty hand-written migration: <version>_<name>.up.sql (comments only, no -- momo:generated), <version>_<name>.snapshot.json (a copy of the latest snapshot with the new version and that snapshot as its parent) and the extended momo.sum. The name follows the diff rule (lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter). It needs an existing snapshot to copy: run diff first (exit 2 otherwise), and it never overwrites a file (exit 1). Write the SQL in the up file, then run momo migrate hash (the file changed after momo.sum was written) and momo migrate validate.

You can also create the files yourself:

  1. Choose a version greater than the latest and a name: 20260301120000_backfill_slug.up.sql. Do not put -- momo:generated in it.
  2. Optional directives at the top, before the first statement: -- momo:no-transaction, -- momo:split, -- momo:destructive (informational, never enforced), -- momo:generated (do not use it here) and -- momo:sqlite-foreign-keys-off (SQLite only; apply turns foreign keys off around the migration, section 3a). -- momo:ddl is not a file directive: it goes before one MySQL ALTER TABLE statement (section 9). An unknown -- momo: directive is an error.
  3. Create 20260301120000_backfill_slug.snapshot.json as a copy of the previous snapshot with version set to the new version and parent set to the previous version. The schema must stay equal to the parent's, or validate reports "custom migration ... must not change the schema".
  4. momo migrate hash, momo migrate validate, then apply.

If the SQL changes the schema, change the models too and run diff afterward, which compares against the latest snapshot as written; otherwise the next diff will try to generate the same change again.

docs.title: 6a. Go migrations
docs.text:
A data step that SQL cannot express (a backfill that calls library code, the templates an application ships in Go) is a migrate.GoMigration. It is registered on the engine with migrate.WithGoMigrations and is ordered with the SQL files by version, so it runs once, under the same lock, with a history row (kind = 'go') like any other migration.

g := migrate.GoMigration{
    Version:  "20260301120000", // 14 digits, unique among the SQL files too
    Name:     "backfill_templates",
    Checksum: "v1", // optional, see below
    Up: func(ctx context.Context, tx *momo.Tx) error {
        _, err := momo.Exec(ctx, tx, `UPDATE company SET templates_ready = true`)
        return err
    },
}
engine, err := migrate.NewEngine(drv, dir, migrate.WithDialect(pg), migrate.WithGoMigrations(g))
  • Transaction. Up receives a *momo.Tx: the migration transaction that also holds the history rows. An error or a panic rolls everything back and records rolled_back (not dirty); the next apply runs it again. The function cannot commit or roll back that transaction.
  • No transaction. Set UpNoTx instead of Up for work that cannot run in a transaction (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, a long backfill committed in batches). It receives a *momo.DB bound to the migration connection (DB.OnConn; it cannot begin a transaction). An error leaves the row failed, which is dirty: apply refuses with ErrDirty until you finish the work by hand and run resolve (section 4). Make the function safe to run again, because resolve --rolled-back runs it from the start.
  • Version. A Go migration and a SQL file cannot share a version; plan, apply and status fail with an error naming the file, and NewEngine rejects two Go migrations on one version or a bad version or name.
  • Checksum. Go code cannot be hashed. The recorded checksum is a hash of the version, the name and the optional Checksum string. When it differs from the applied row, apply refuses with ErrChecksumMismatch and status shows mismatch. Bump Checksum when you change what a migration does and want an already-migrated database flagged; leave it empty to bind only version and name.
  • Snapshot. A Go migration has a snapshot file like a custom SQL migration (<version>_<name>.snapshot.json, a copy of the previous snapshot with the new version and parent set), and no up file. It must not change the schema. migrate.ValidateOffline checks that when you pass it the registered migrations after the directory, and that every registered Go migration has a snapshot; run it from a test of the application with the same migrations. momo migrate validate does not know the application's Go migrations, so it cannot check them. diff compares against the latest snapshot, a Go migration's included, and refuses while a registered Go migration has no snapshot file yet. Note for callers: ValidateOffline gained a variadic parameter, so a call without Go migrations compiles unchanged, but a function value of the old type no longer matches.
  • Forward only. A Go migration has no down step. A rollback of the group that contains one refuses it: Engine.Rollback (landing from the M1 migrations branch) calls migrate.RefuseGoRollback with the history rows to roll back, which returns ErrGoMigrationNotReversible for the first row of kind go; fix forward with a new migration.
  • Baseline. Baseline through a version records a go row (checksum = the identity) for every registered Go migration up to it. An engine without that registration, the CLI included, refuses to baseline past a snapshot-only version with ErrGoMigrationUnregistered, because it cannot record the row.
  • Hooks and options. Without migrate.WithGoMigrationDB, Up and UpNoTx get a bare momo.New of the engine's driver: none of the application's hooks, field hooks, clock or other options. Pass the application's *momo.DB (same driver) to WithGoMigrationDB to have its options apply.
  • The CLI cannot run them, and refuses to pass them. momo migrate apply, plan and status read only the directory; a Go migration lives in the application's binary. The snapshot file marks its place: when the directory holds a snapshot with no up file, no registered Go migration and no history row, and a pending SQL migration has a later version, apply refuses with ErrGoMigrationUnregistered (exit 1) before it runs anything, telling you to run the application's Engine.Apply. Without that, the CLI would apply the later SQL and the application's engine would then fail with ErrOutOfOrder for the Go migration for good. Once the Go migration is applied, the CLI is unblocked; a database that has one in its history shows it as missing to the CLI. The check keys on the snapshot file, so a Go migration whose snapshot file is missing is invisible to the CLI: run ValidateOffline with your Go migrations in a test of the application, which reports that. The same refusal fires for an up file that was removed and left its snapshot, so when you squash old migrations remove their snapshots too. The application runs the engine itself, at start or in a small cmd/migrate of its own:
eng, err := migrate.NewEngine(drv, dir, migrate.WithDialect(pg), migrate.WithGoMigrations(g))
if err != nil { /* ... */ }
if _, err := eng.Apply(ctx, migrate.ApplyOptions{}); err != nil { /* ... */ }

Use that binary for apply, and keep the CLI for diff, hash, validate and drift.

docs.title: 7. Adopting an existing database
docs.text:
Worked example: examples/adopt-existing-schema.

momo generate --from-db reads a live PostgreSQL database and writes the models and the init snapshot, so nothing has to be written by hand first.

  1. Run momo generate --from-db DATABASE_URL. The value is a database URL, - to read the URL from standard input, or the name of an environment variable that holds it; prefer the last two, because a URL on the command line is visible in the process list. It inspects the schemas named by migrate.schemas (default: the current schema), writes one <table>_model.go per table into the model package (--out, else introspect.out, else the first local entry of packages, else ./models) and, when the migration directory has no snapshot, the init migration and snapshot. Do not apply the init migration.
  2. Run momo generate, which writes the generated code for the new models.
  3. momo migrate baseline --version <init version>. It checks the live database against that snapshot, including view, policy and trigger text, and exits 1 with differing object kinds: ... on a mismatch, then records every migration up to that version as applied with statements_applied = 0 and apply_id = baseline, without running them. --force records anyway; use it only after reviewing the mismatch. Schema objects outside the models, such as extra extensions, count as a mismatch: add them to migrate.exclude. The run prints a hint for the extensions and skipped tables it found.
  4. From then on use diff and apply.
