The models carry exact table and column names (a table or column tag is written wherever the naming preset would derive another name), Go types, nullability (a pointer, or the nullable tag for slices), defaults, size, precision and scale, enums, primary keys, identity and serial columns, single-column indexes as tags, other indexes, unique constraints, checks and comments in the MomoConfig method, and every foreign key the generator can derive as a belongs_to field with its on_delete and on_update actions. numeric columns are Go strings (the decimal-as-string note); an introspect.types rule picks a decimal type instead.

A column type with no Go mapping is an error and nothing is written; add a rule to the introspect section of momo.yaml. Constraints the models cannot declare are left out of the models and the snapshot and printed as warnings, so the two agree and the baseline reports them: composite foreign keys, foreign keys whose name is not table, column and _fkey, foreign keys that do not reference a single-column primary key, unique expression indexes, generated columns, generated always identity (modeled as by default), and PostgreSQL schemas other than the current one.

docs.title: The introspect section
docs.text:
momo.yaml holds what the database cannot say, and it is applied again on every run:

introspect:
  package: models # default: the directory name
  out: ./models # default: the first local entry of packages
  skip: ["_prisma_*"] # table globs: no model, not in the snapshot
  types: # SQL type to Go type, for every column of that type
    inet: { go: string }
    numeric(12,2):
      { go: decimal.Decimal, import: github.com/shopspring/decimal }
  columns: # first to last; later rules win, tags add up
    - match: "*.updated_at" # glob over table.column
      tags: [updated_at]
    - match: "users.settings"
      go: "types.JSON[Settings]"
      name: Prefs # Go field name
  tables:
    users: { name: Account, tags: ["soft_delete:timestamp"] }

A rule's tags are momo tag options; one with the key of a generated option replaces it. A Go type needs no import for types., vector., time., json. or sql.. Add skipped tables to migrate.exclude too, so the baseline ignores the live tables.

docs.title: Running it again
docs.text:
The schema keeps changing during a port. A re-run rewrites the model files that nobody edited. Each file starts with a header that holds the hash of its body: when the body still matches, the file is regenerated freely. A file with hand edits, or one that --from-db did not write, is never replaced. A hand-edited file stays quiet while the database has not changed its model; it conflicts only when the regenerated model differs. The run writes the regenerated version next to it as <file>.new, prints conflict: <file>, and exits 1; merge the two by hand and delete the .new file, or run again with --overwrite to take the regenerated one. --overwrite only replaces a conflicting file: an edited file whose model the database did not change stays as it is. A file whose table is gone is printed as orphan and never deleted. --check writes nothing, prints stale: <file> for each difference and exits 1. The init snapshot is written once: when the migration directory already has a snapshot, use diff for later schema changes. Put code of your own in other files and rules in the introspect section, and a re-run stays quiet.

baseline needs CREATE on the database for the canonicalization step when the snapshot has views, functions, triggers or policies, or any table with text PostgreSQL rewrites: a column default or generation expression, a check constraint, an index predicate or an index expression. A snapshot of plain tables, columns, keys and plain indexes needs no such privilege (TestBaselineAsAppRole). --force does not waive it: the error is ErrCanonicalizePrivilege, naming the privilege, and nothing is recorded (TestBaselineAsAppRoleNeedsCreateForTableText). Run the baseline once as a role that has CREATE on the database (for example the owner role), or grant it for that run. It takes the lock and refuses on dirty or checksum problems like apply.

docs.title: Roles and extensions (verified)
docs.text:
Checked on CI with a role that is not a superuser and has no CREATE on the database:

  • CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector succeeds when the extension already exists (PostgreSQL only emits a notice; it checks existence before privileges). So the statement that a generated migration emits is harmless for that role once a superuser has installed pgvector (TestAppRoleExtensionIfNotExists). When the extension is not installed the statement needs a privileged role, as before.
  • baseline and apply run CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS for the history table. PostgreSQL checks CREATE on the schema before it looks for the table, so a role with only USAGE on the schema is refused with the error permission denied for schema even when it owns an existing momo_migrations (TestBaselineAsAppRoleNeedsCreateOnSchema). The migrator role needs CREATE on its schema: GRANT CREATE ON SCHEMA app TO app_role.
  • With CREATE on the schema but not on the database, baseline works for a snapshot without table text (TestBaselineAsAppRole) and fails with ErrCanonicalizePrivilege otherwise (section 7).

docs.title: Extensions managed outside momo
docs.text:
Set migrate.external_extensions in momo.yaml for an extension that a superuser installs by hand:

migrate:
  external_extensions: [vector]

Names are exact. For each listed extension momo

  • never emits CREATE EXTENSION from diff (or AutoMigrate), even when a model has a vector column, and keeps it out of the snapshot it writes;
  • does not report it from drift, and does not count it as a mismatch in baseline, even though the live database has it.

The migrations then no longer create the extension, so a new environment must get it before the first apply. Use it only when that is the intent. It differs from migrate.exclude, which hides unmanaged objects of every kind from drift and baseline but does not stop diff from emitting CREATE EXTENSION for a model that needs it. If a snapshot already declares the extension, the setting hides it on both sides, so no drop or create is generated either.

A database that uses serial or bigserial ids is adopted with the serial tag, as in pk,serial on an int64 field. The tag renders smallserial, serial or bigserial by the Go integer width. Inspection reads a column whose default is nextval of a sequence owned by the column back as the same serial column, so the snapshot matches and diff stays empty. serial is PostgreSQL only; other dialects refuse it. Turning an existing column into or out of serial is refused by diff, with an error that asks for a hand-written migration.

Upgrade note: inspection used to report a serial column as identity. If you adopted a serial database with pk,identity on the model, or kept a snapshot taken from one, diff now stops with column "id" is a serial column in the database but the model declares identity. Change the tag to pk,serial and regenerate the snapshot; or write a migration that converts the column to identity. Momo does not treat the two as equal, because a new environment would then be built with identity while production keeps its serial.

AutoMigrate is a Go API for development and tests. It applies additive changes only, writes no history and no files, and returns the rest as Skipped. Do not mix it with versioned migrations on one schema.

docs.title: 7a. Cutover from Prisma db push to momo
docs.text:
Playbook for a database whose schema is changed by prisma db push and hand-written idempotent SQL files (DO $$ ... IF NOT EXISTS guards, GRANT lines, a hand-created extension), moving to momo owning the DDL. Rehearse every step on a copy of production.

  1. Models first. Write the momo models so they match the live database (section 7). Columns Prisma generates in the client, such as cuid ids, are not in the database; model them as plain columns.
  2. Declare what you do not own. Put the extension a superuser installs in migrate.external_extensions. Put tables, views and functions that stay outside the models (an analytics schema, an audit table, Prisma's _prisma_migrations) in migrate.exclude. Roles, grants and sequences outside a column are not part of the schema model; they stay in hand-written SQL.
  3. Write the initial migration. momo migrate diff init against an empty directory. Do not apply it. Read the generated SQL: it is what a new environment would run, and it must build the schema you have.
  4. Rehearse the baseline on a copy, with momo migrate baseline --version <init version>, as a role with CREATE on the database (section 7). Exit 1 lists the differing object kinds. Fix the models or exclude until it is clean. Do not use --force to skip a difference you have not read.
  5. Dual-writer period: momo watches, it does not write. While Prisma still pushes, the database moves under momo. Do not baseline production yet and do not apply migrations. Run momo migrate drift against a baselined copy, or the rehearsal in step 4 against production, on a schedule. A table Prisma added shows as unmanaged:, a new column in a managed table as changed: ... not in snapshot, and an altered column as changed:. Each is a task: put it in the models, or in exclude. Drift cannot see changed view, trigger or policy text (section 1).
  6. Freeze db push. Stop prisma db push in every environment (remove it from the deploy). Update the models to the final live state and, since nothing was applied, delete the unapplied init files and run diff init again, so the initial snapshot is the schema as it is at the freeze.
  7. Baseline each environment. In each environment run momo migrate baseline --version <init version> once, then momo migrate drift (expect no drift). The role that runs apply needs CREATE on the schema (section 7). From then on apply runs only newer migrations. A database created from scratch runs the init migration; it needs the external extension installed first.
  8. Hand off. Schema changes go through diff; backfills and other data changes through momo migrate new --custom, which replaces the hand-written SQL files. Leave guards such as IF NOT EXISTS out of new files: the history says what ran.

Undo: baseline only writes history rows, so drop the momo_migrations table to return to the state before step 7; nothing else changed.

docs.title: 8. Security
docs.text:
• momo redacts connection strings from everything it prints (stdout, stderr, error text, and bad flag values that a pasted URL lands in): URL userinfo becomes ***@, a URL in text that has a query keeps the part before ? and shows ?***, a password=/passwd=/pwd= value becomes ***, and the exact URL and password given are replaced by ***. History error text is the server message only, never Detail. Messages of SQLSTATE class 22 (data exception) are withheld because they can contain data values. Connection URLs and password= values in the text are replaced by *** before it is stored (TestHistoryErrorIsRedacted).
  • A warning on stderr (not a failure) when a command that needs a database is given a URL with sslmode=disable and any non-local host: TLS is not enforced (sslmode=disable) for remote host H: credentials and data can cross the network unencrypted; use sslmode=verify-full. It names the hosts only. It also fires when the URL or key=value string has no sslmode (libpq then uses prefer, which falls back to plaintext), for allow and prefer, for key=value connection strings, and when sslmode comes from PGSSLMODE; a host missing from the string is read from PGHOST. localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, unix socket paths and no host at all do not warn, and neither do require, verify-ca and verify-full. require encrypts but does not check the server's identity, so use sslmode=verify-full against a real server.
  • Do not pass the URL with --url on shared hosts (momo warns); use migrate.url_env, MOMO_DATABASE_URL or --url - (stdin).
  • Review *.up.sql in code review like any code: apply runs it as the connected role, and momo.sum only detects change, not intent.
  • Tamper detection is against accidental edits, not an attacker. momo migrate hash rewrites momo.sum to match whatever is on disk, and momo migrate rehash --accept stores the checksum of whatever file is on disk in the history row. Both trust the files completely: anyone who can edit the migration files and run those commands can make an edited migration pass every check. Protect the migration directory with code review and write access control, and the database with the migrator role's grants; momo.sum does not.
  • drift and baseline execute model DDL on the target database. To compare declared text with what the database reports, they create a scratch schema and run the declared definitions (defaults, checks, index predicates, view queries, function bodies, policy and trigger expressions) in a transaction that is rolled back. That needs CREATE on the database, runs SQL taken from your snapshots and models, and takes locks while it runs. Run them against a scratch database restored from a backup, or a clone, rather than production.

docs.title: 9. MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text:
The migrate/mysql package is the migration dialect for MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7 and MariaDB 11.8. It reads information_schema, renders DDL and locks with GET_LOCK. momo migrate does not select it yet; build the engine with migrate.WithDialect(mmysql.New()) and the mysqldriver driver; the command line is PostgreSQL-only.

Every migration is non-transactional. DDL implies a commit on these servers, so a failure cannot be rolled back. The engine runs each statement on its own, records statements_applied after each one, and leaves a failed row that is dirty until you repair the database and run resolve. This holds with or without -- momo:no-transaction, for Go migrations, and for rollback: a down that fails half-way leaves its earlier statements applied and the row failed. Write each migration so that a half-applied run is easy to finish by hand.

Locking. GET_LOCK names are server-wide, so the lock name carries the database (momo:<database>.momo_migrations, cut to the 64 characters MySQL allows, with a hash suffix when the key is longer). The lock belongs to the pinned connection and is released with RELEASE_LOCK, or when the connection ends. A busy lock returns migrate.ErrLocked with the connection id of the holder.

Session timeouts. The lock timeout becomes lock_wait_timeout, the time a statement waits for a metadata lock, in whole seconds. A statement timeout becomes max_statement_time on MariaDB; on MySQL it is refused with momo.ErrUnsupported, because max_execution_time bounds SELECT only.

Online DDL. A line -- momo:ddl ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE directly before an ALTER TABLE statement appends those options to it. MySQL rejects LOCK=NONE together with ALGORITHM=INSTANT; use ALGORITHM=INSTANT alone. The server rejects the statement when it cannot honour them, so a change that would copy the table fails instead of running slowly. Without the directive momo adds no ALGORITHM or LOCK clause. Only ALGORITHM= and LOCK= options are accepted.

What inspection reports. One database is inspected, the connection's default, and the history table is left out.

  • A UNIQUE constraint and a unique index are the same object on these servers. A unique key made of plain ascending columns is reported as a unique constraint; declare such keys as constraints.
  • The index MySQL creates for a foreign key, named after the constraint, is not reported, and the diff refuses a declared index that has the name of a foreign key of its table, because the two would collide and could not be told apart. An index of a database you adopt that already has such a name and the key's columns is treated as the server's own.
  • NO ACTION is reported as an empty action. MariaDB reports its default as RESTRICT, so on MariaDB RESTRICT and an unwritten clause are one.
  • MariaDB stores json as longtext with a json_valid check named after the column; the pair is reported as type json.
  • A column is reported with a collation only when it differs from its table's default; declare Collate on the column to pin one.
  • Defaults that the servers store alike are one default: NOW, LOCALTIME and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP; TRUE and FALSE are 1 and 0. RESTRICT and NO ACTION are the same foreign key action.
  • Stored CHECK text is compared without the identifier quotes, character set introducers and the parentheses MySQL adds around each comparison. Other rewrites by the server (for example != stored as <>) show as a difference of text; write the expression the way the server stores it. Parentheses around a comparison are removed only between and, or and xor, so (a between 1 and 2) and c > 0 keeps them and differs from the same text without them; a backslash escape inside a string is kept as written.
  • A foreign key into another database is reported as database.table.
  • Integer display widths (int(11) on MariaDB) are no difference of type. Identifier quotes, character set introducers and outer parentheses in stored expressions are no difference of text.
  • An index part with a prefix length is the column name followed by the length in parentheses, such as name(10). Index visibility, character sets and ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are not part of the schema model, and a MODIFY COLUMN that a type change renders restates the column without them: an ALTER of such a column is a migration to write by hand.

Rendering. Tables are ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4. An identity column is AUTO_INCREMENT (by_default; always and serial are refused). A default that is not a literal or CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is wrapped in parentheses, as MySQL requires. Partial indexes, storage parameters, operator classes, enums, views, functions, triggers and policies have no MySQL rendering yet and are refused. The hash index method is refused: InnoDB builds it as BTREE. Dropping a foreign key also drops the index MySQL built for it, when one exists, unless another foreign key of the table starts with the same column: that key may rely on the index, and dropping it would fail after the key was gone. The index then stays and shows as an index named like the dropped key; declare it, or drop it once nothing needs it. An AUTO_INCREMENT column must be a key in the statement that adds it, but the engine adds a primary key in a separate statement after the column: add such a column and its key in a migration you write yourself. Declare a generated column as nullable: MariaDB does not take NOT NULL on one. MySQL refuses a CHECK, or a stored generated column, on a column that a foreign key with a referential action uses.

docs.title: Upgrading: generated file header
docs.text:
Generated Go files start with // Code generated by momo (format 1). DO NOT EDIT.. The header carries the generated-file format number, which decides compatibility, and no momo release version, so a later momo upgrade does not rewrite generated files whose code is unchanged. Earlier releases wrote // Code generated by momo v0.1.0-dev (format 1). DO NOT EDIT.; momo still recognises that form, so orphan detection keeps working.

After upgrading, run momo generate once. Until then momo generate --check reports the header change in every generated file.

docs.text:
Each is filed as a bug story in .procoder/backlog/stories/<id>.md.

None open. Fixed issues are listed in the changelog.

docs.title: momovet: static check for raw SQL
docs.text: Momo binds every value as a parameter, but the raw-SQL functions take the statement text as a Go string. A string built with + or a format call from user input is an injection point. The momovet analyzer reports it.

docs.title: What it reports
docs.text:
A call to one of these functions of github.com/azrtydxb/momo whose SQL argument is not a constant:

Function SQL argument momo.Exec third (after the context and the querier) momo.Scalars third (after the context and the querier) momo.MapRows third (after the context and the querier) momo.SQL first momo.TypedSQL first momo.RawSubquery first

A constant is a string literal, a const, or an expression made only of constants ("UPDATE t SET " + "x = 1"). Anything else is reported as non-constant SQL string passed to momo.<Name>. Pass values as arguments after the SQL text instead of concatenating them.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
go install github.com/azrtydxb/momo/cmd/momovet@latest
go vet -vettool="$(which momovet)" ./...

It also runs standalone: momovet ./....

To embed it in your own multichecker, import github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momovet and use its Analyzer variable.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The analyzer does not follow assignments. A var that holds a literal is reported, even a package-level one that is never reassigned: this is a false positive by design, so declare it as a const. It checks the call site only, so SQL built in one function and passed through another is reported where it reaches a raw-SQL function.

docs.title: MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text: What works on MySQL and MariaDB today, and what does not. The driver is driver/mysqldriver (database/sql on github.com/go-sql-driver/mysql). The migration dialect migrate/mysql exists as a library; the momo migrate command is PostgreSQL-only (see Migrations).

docs.title: Supported servers
docs.text:
Server Version Image used in CI MySQL 8.4 LTS 8.4.13 mysql:8.4.13 MySQL 9.7 LTS 9.7.4 mysql:9.7.4 MariaDB 11.8 LTS 11.8.9 mariadb:11.8.9

No innovation releases are supported. CI runs the shared suites against all three servers (the integration-mysql job), on every push.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Open the pool with mysqldriver.Open(dsn, flavor), or build the DSN with mysqldriver.ConfigureDSN and pass the *sql.DB to mysqldriver.New. The configured DSN always has:

  • parseTime=true and loc=UTC, and the session time_zone set to +00:00;
  • clientFoundRows=true, so an UPDATE reports the rows it matched;
  • interpolateParams=false and multiStatements=false: values always travel as bound parameters of a prepared statement and never become SQL text. A DSN that sets either is overridden. A *sql.DB handed to New directly must already be configured this way.

Open pings the server, as the SQLite drivers do, so a bad DSN, a refused connection or bad credentials fail at Open and not on the first statement. An unknown flavor makes Open return ErrUnsupported; on any error the pool is closed and nothing is returned. (New, which takes an already opened *sql.DB, still returns a driver whose every call is ErrUnsupported for an unknown flavor, because it has no error to return.)

ConfigureDSN (and so Open) refuses two DSN settings with ErrValidation:

  • allowAllFiles=true, which lets the server read any client file through LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE;
  • allowCleartextPasswords=true, which sends the password unhashed.

Remove them from the DSN. The error message never quotes the DSN.

Transport security is the DSN's business and defaults to none: add tls=true (or a registered TLS config) for any server that is not on the same host.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
The rows below are checked against dialect.MySQLFlavor by TestCapabilityMatrixMatchesDialect.

Capability mysql mariadb Returning no no InsertReturning no yes OnConflict no no OnDuplicateKey yes yes NullsOrdering no no TransactionalDDL no no Merge no no ILike no no

Returning is the UPDATE and DELETE form. MariaDB 11.8 can return rows from an INSERT only (INSERT ... RETURNING), which is why it has InsertReturning set while Returning stays false: Returning on an insert works on MariaDB, and on an update or delete it is ErrUnsupported on both servers. MySQL has no RETURNING at all.

docs.title: Writes
docs.text:
• A single Model insert reads LAST_INSERT_ID and writes it into the identity field of the model. A key generated on the Go side (an id generator) always wins; LAST_INSERT_ID is read only for a key the database generates. A multi-row insert returns and writes back no keys, because the ids of a multi-row statement depend on innodb_autoinc_lock_mode. On MariaDB, ask for them with Returning; on MySQL that is ErrUnsupported. The LAST_INSERT_ID write-back does not apply to an upsert or to any insert with a conflict clause (wantsGeneratedKey in the core is false for them), because the statement may update an existing row and LAST_INSERT_ID then does not name the row's key; read the row back with a query.
  • Upserts render as INSERT ... VALUES ... AS momo_new ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE on MySQL and with VALUES(col) on MariaDB. DoNothing renders a no-op assignment of a key column. A Where on a conflict clause is ErrUnsupported.
  • ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE fires for a conflict on any unique key and cannot name one. Momo therefore accepts a conflict target only when it is the only unique key of the table, the primary key included; otherwise the call is ErrUnsupported. Without a schema (a hand-written model) only a primary-key target is accepted.
  • With clientFoundRows, an upsert reports 1 for an inserted row, 2 for an existing row that changed, and 1 for an existing row set to its current values. DoNothing also reports 1 for a skipped row. A count of 1 does not tell an insert from a skip.
  • A bare OFFSET gets LIMIT 18446744073709551615 in front of it, because MySQL and MariaDB reject an offset without a limit.

docs.title: Locking and transactions
docs.text: ForUpdate and ForShare render FOR UPDATE and FOR SHARE; NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED are passed through. MariaDB 11.8 has no FOR SHARE, so it gets LOCK IN SHARE MODE. LockOf (FOR UPDATE OF) is MySQL only; on MariaDB it is ErrUnsupported. Savepoints and the four standard isolation levels work; read-only transactions use START TRANSACTION READ ONLY. Any other isolation level is ErrUnsupported.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Server errors map by number: 1062 unique, 1451 and 1452 (and 1216, 1217) foreign key, 1048 and 1364 not null, 3819 (MySQL) and 4025 (MariaDB) check, 1213 and MariaDB 1020 serialization (deadlock, and a row that changed under innodb_snapshot_isolation), 1205 and 3572 busy. Error() never shows the server text, which can quote a row value; Detail() returns it, and errors.As reaches the *mysql.MySQLError. The constraint name differs by server: MySQL 8 reports a unique key as table.index, MariaDB reports only the index name.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text: MySQL 8.4 has no vector columns. MySQL 9.7 stores VECTOR and reads it back, but offers no distance function in the Community edition (DISTANCE() is HeatWave and MySQL AI only), so every distance builder is ErrUnsupported on MySQL. MariaDB 11.8 renders L2Distance as VEC_DISTANCE_EUCLIDEAN and CosineDistance as VEC_DISTANCE_COSINE on vector.Vector columns, and its driver reports Vectors. Inner product, L1, Hamming, Jaccard and the half, sparse and bit types return ErrUnsupported on MariaDB. Details and the VECTOR INDEX rules are in vectors.md.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: The library dialect migrate/mysql inspects information_schema, renders DDL, locks with GET_LOCK and runs every migration, up and down, statement by statement, because DDL commits implicitly on these servers. Build the engine with migrate.WithDialect and the mysqldriver driver; the inspector, drift check and -- momo:ddl online DDL options work through it. The momo migrate command still builds only the PostgreSQL dialect, so it rejects MySQL and MariaDB. What the dialect reports and renders is in migrations.md.

docs.title: Projections
docs.text: A projection is a result type that is not a table: a subset of a table's columns, an aggregate, or a computed column such as a vector distance. You select it with momo.Select[T], name the source with From and the select list with Columns. A projection is read only: it cannot be inserted, updated or deleted.

docs.title: Declaring one
docs.text:
Embed momo.Projection by value in a struct. Every exported field is one column of the select list, in declaration order.

type Card struct {
    momo.Projection
    ID    int64
    Title string
    Score int64 `momo:"column:points"`
}
  • The column name of a field follows the naming rule of the project (naming: in momo.yaml), as for model fields. A momo:"column:..." tag overrides it. The name is a label: the select list is positional and not aliased.
  • Unexported fields and fields tagged momo:"-" are skipped. Relation tags are an error on a projection.
  • A projection has no table, no primary key, no indexes and no MomoConfig. The generator does not add it to the schema, so it never appears in a migration.
  • A field type must be one the generator maps (see the type mapping). An unsupported type fails momo generate with a message that names the struct and the field, for example projection Odd: field Value: Go type complex128 has no SQL mapping.

docs.title: The generated metadata
docs.text: momo generate writes, for each projection, a MomoMeta method and a momo.Meta value into the momo_gen.go of the package that declares it. Columns, Ptr and Value cover every field in declaration order. Identity, Version, SoftDelete, CreatedAt and UpdatedAt are all -1, because a projection has none of those columns. Do not write this by hand. A package that holds only projections gets a momo_gen.go too.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
cards, err := momo.Select[models.Card](q).
    From(article.Table).
    Columns(article.ID, article.Title, article.Score).
    OrderBy(article.Score.Desc(), article.ID.Asc()).
    All(ctx)

From takes the generated Table of a model package, an aliased table (article.Table.As("a")), a CTE or a subquery. Columns must list as many expressions as the struct has fields, in field order. Without Columns the query fails with ErrValidation. Computed expressions (a distance, momo.CountAll()) are valid entries.

Keyset pagination over a projection lists the unique tie-break key in OrderBy yourself, since the metadata has no primary key. See projection-pagination.

docs.title: Tuple rows: no struct per shape
docs.text:
For an aggregate, a join or a few columns that you read in one place, skip the struct and the generated metadata: momo.Row1 to momo.Row10 are generic projections with fields C1 to Cn. Columns is scanned positionally, so expression i fills Ci.

// a count per key
rows, err := momo.Select[momo.Row2[string, int64]](db).
    From(license.Table).
    Columns(license.Key, momo.CountAll()).
    GroupBy(license.Key).
    All(ctx)
for _, r := range rows {
    fmt.Println(r.C1, r.C2) // key, count
}

// a single aggregate
total, err := momo.Select[momo.Row1[int64]](db).From(license.Table).Columns(momo.CountAll()).One(ctx)
// total.C1
  • A column that can be NULL takes a pointer type: a LeftJoin side or an aggregate over no rows. With a Row3 of string, *int64, *string, the columns a.Title, b.ID, b.Title fill C1 to C3, and C2 and C3 stay nil when the join finds no row.
  • Subquery columns, Union, FromSubquery, With and WithRecursive work as for any projection. The Go types of the columns are yours to match; they are not checked against the SQL.
  • A mismatch between the number of Columns and the arity of the row is ErrValidation, reported before any statement runs. So is omitting Columns.
  • A tuple row is a projection with no table: Insert, Update, Delete, Upsert, SoftDelete and ForceDelete refuse it with ErrValidation. It has no soft-delete column of its own, and the filter on the From table applies as described below, so a Row1[int64] with CountAll over article.Table counts live rows, and WithDeleted counts all.
  • After works when OrderBy lists a unique key, since a tuple has no primary key to break ties.
  • The metadata is built once per instantiation and shared; looking it up does not allocate.

When the result has meaning worth a name, or more than ten columns, declare a projection struct instead and let momo generate write its metadata.

docs.title: Soft-deleted rows
docs.text:
When From is the generated Table of a model that has a soft-delete column (timestamp, unix or bool), a projection excludes soft-deleted rows by default, exactly as a model query does. WithDeleted() includes them and OnlyDeleted() returns only them. Do not add the deleted_at predicate by hand.

The filter applies to the From table whatever else the query does: with Join or LeftJoin the From table is still filtered, and the joined tables are not (filter them in the ON clause or a Where, as for a model). To alias the table keep the generated one and call As: article.Table.As("a") keeps the soft-delete column, so the filter is qualified with the alias.

The filter is not added when:

  • From is a subquery or CTE: filter inside it;
  • From is a hand-built momo.TableRef{Name: ..., Alias: ...}: it carries no soft-delete column. Start from the generated article.Table instead, or add the predicate yourself, for example Where(article.DeletedAt.IsNull()).

docs.title: Upgrading from hand-written metadata
docs.text: Before the generator emitted projections, the guides told you to write MomoMeta and a momo.Meta value for each projection by hand. After you upgrade, momo generate writes them too, and the package no longer compiles (MomoMeta redeclared). Delete the hand-written MomoMeta method and its Meta variable for every struct that embeds momo.Projection, then run momo generate. Check that the field order and momo:"column:..." tags give the column names you had. Remove any Where(<table>.DeletedAt.IsNull()) you added to projection queries; keeping it is harmless but redundant.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
This guide covers how Momo models relations between tables: declaring them, loading them, filtering by them, writing them, and observing them. Every snippet uses the real API. The models are a small document store: Document belongs to an Author, has many Comments, and is tagged with many Tags.

Relation operations are methods and functions on the generated Relation[P, C] descriptor, where P is the parent model and C the child model. A descriptor is immutable and safe for concurrent use.

  • Declaring relations
  • Eager loading
  • Preload and single-query loading
  • Pipelined loading
  • Relation predicates and traversal
  • Association helpers
  • Graph writes
  • Observability
  • Errors and limitations

docs.title: 1. Declaring relations
docs.text:
A relation is a field on the parent model. Its tag names the kind, and the Go type of the field decides the shape:

Tag Field type Foreign key lives on belongs_to *Target the parent has_one *Target the child has_many []Target the child many2many []Target a join table 
type Author struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:authors"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Name       string

    Documents []Document `momo:"has_many,fk:AuthorID"`
}

type Document struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:documents"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    AuthorID   *int64
    Title      string

    Author   *Author   `momo:"belongs_to,fk:AuthorID"`
    Comments []Comment `momo:"has_many,fk:DocumentID"`
    Tags     []Tag     `momo:"many2many,join:taggings"`
}

type Comment struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:comments"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    DocumentID int64
    Body       string
    Approved   bool
}

type Tag struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:tags"`
    ID         int64 `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Name       string
}

The generated code lives in one package per model (author, document, comment, tag), imported next to the models package.

docs.title: Generating relation code
docs.text:
Run momo generate in the module that holds your models (or add //go:generate momo generate to a source file and run go generate ./...). It reads momo.yaml and writes the descriptors into the model packages. Commit the generated files, and use momo generate --check in CI to catch stale ones. The README walks through the setup in Configure and generate. The join tables and foreign keys come from momo migrate diff and momo migrate apply, see Create and apply the migration.

Tag options for relations:

  • fk:<Field> is required for belongs_to, has_one and has_many. For belongs_to it names the foreign-key field on the parent (the model that declares the relation). For has_one and has_many it names the field on the child.
  • join:<table> is required for many2many. The join columns are named after each model and its primary key column, for example document_id and tag_id. Rules:
  • Set join: (same table) on every many2many side you declare. The reverse side is optional, but a reverse side declared without join: makes the generator report a diagnostic.
  • A many-to-many to the model's own type is not supported.
  • Both models need a primary key.
  • The join table has exactly two key columns, named <model>_<pkcol>. Extra join-table columns are not modelled by this guide; use an explicit join model such as a Tagging struct for those.
  • polytype:<column> together with polyvalue:<value> makes a has_one or has_many polymorphic: the child row belongs to the parent only when its type column equals the value.
  • on_delete, on_update and no_constraint affect only the foreign key emitted for belongs_to. has_one and has_many create no constraint, and many-to-many join tables always get two foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE.

momo generate reads these tags and writes one descriptor per relation field into the model's package. The descriptor holds the relation name and kind, the parent and child tables, the key columns, Through for the join table of a many-to-many relation, Discriminator for a polymorphic one, and the typed functions that read and write keys and the field itself. You refer to a relation as <model package>.<Field>:

document.Author   // belongs-to: momo.Relation[models.Document, models.Author]
document.Comments // has-many
document.Tags     // many-to-many

The generator reports a diagnostic, and writes nothing for that package, when:

  • a relation has more than one kind, or the field type does not match the kind;
  • the target is not a Momo model;
  • fk is missing, or names a field that does not exist;
  • many2many has no join:, or a declared reverse side has no join:;
  • polytype is given without polyvalue or the other way round, or polytype is used on a relation that is not has_one or has_many;
  • the polytype column is not a field of the target.

A belongs_to is keyed by its own fk field against the target's primary key, so the referencing model may have any primary key, including a composite one that contains the foreign key column. For example exams with primary key (license_id, exam_id) can declare License *License with momo:"belongs_to,fk:LicenseID", which emits a foreign key from license_id to the licenses table's license_id column and matches a live database that already has that constraint. The target of a belongs_to must have a single-column primary key: a foreign key to a composite target key is refused with a diagnostic that names the target's key columns. A has_one or has_many needs a single-column primary key on the parent, and the child may have a composite key. many2many needs a single-column primary key on both models. Other composite-key relations work with hand-written descriptors but cannot be expressed with tags.

Generated relation field values (Document.Comments) are only ever written by Momo when you load them or list them for CreateGraph. A plain Insert or Update never touches a relation field.

docs.title: 2. Eager loading
docs.text:
momo.Load loads one relation for a slice of parents and assigns the result onto each element. momo.LoadAll loads several.

docs, err := momo.Select[models.Document](db).Limit(20).All(ctx)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := momo.Load(ctx, db, docs, document.Comments); err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := momo.LoadAll(ctx, db, docs, document.Author, document.Tags); err != nil {
    return err
}

The cost is one statement per relation (per bind-limit chunk, see Chunking), not one per parent. Parent order and length never change. Parents with a NULL key get an empty association: a nil pointer or a nil slice.

Behavior to rely on:

  • Associations are cleared before anything is assigned. A parent that matches no children ends up empty rather than stale, and a load that fails part-way leaves empty associations, never partial ones.
  • Soft-deleted children are excluded by default when the child model has a soft-delete column, as in Select.
  • A to-one child shared by several parents is copied shallowly for each parent. Pointers inside the child, including relations loaded with Then, are shared among those copies.
  • A has-one relation that matches more than one child for a parent fails with ErrTooManyRows.
  • With no parents, LoadAll returns nil and runs nothing.

docs.title: Scoping a load
docs.text:
Relation.Scope takes load options for the child statement:

Option Effect LoadWhere[C] extra predicates on the child table LoadOrderBy[C] child order; the relation key and child primary key are always appended as tie-breakers, so order is stable LoadPerParentLimit[C] keep at most n children per parent (top-N) LoadWithDeleted[C] include soft-deleted children LoadOnlyDeleted[C] only soft-deleted children

Load accepts the same options directly after the relation. Use Scope when you pass the relation to LoadAll or Preload:

err := momo.Load(ctx, db, docs, document.Comments,
    momo.LoadWhere[models.Comment](comment.Approved.Eq(true)),
    momo.LoadOrderBy[models.Comment](comment.ID.Desc()),
    momo.LoadPerParentLimit[models.Comment](3),
)

err = momo.LoadAll(ctx, db, docs,
    document.Author,
    document.Comments.Scope(momo.LoadPerParentLimit[models.Comment](3)),
)

LoadWhere filters before the per-parent limit is applied, so "the three newest approved comments" is what the example above loads.

LoadPerParentLimit uses a window function, so the load stays one statement per chunk. It needs PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, MariaDB 10.2 or SQLite 3.25 or later. It applies to has-many and many-to-many relations only. On belongs-to and has-one it fails with ErrUnsupported, and a negative n fails with ErrValidation, both before any statement runs. Zero means unlimited. For a many-to-many relation whose child has a primary key, duplicated join-table rows share a rank and cannot use up the limit. Without a child primary key, each duplicated row takes a rank and can count against the limit.

LoadWithDeleted and LoadOnlyDeleted replace each other: the last one given wins. They have no effect on a child model without a soft-delete column.

docs.title: Nested loads
docs.text:
Relation.Then loads relations on the children, in one pass over all children of the level above:

err := momo.LoadAll(ctx, db, authors,
    author.Documents.Then(document.Comments),
)

Nested loads run over the children that were kept, so combined with a per-parent limit they only load for the survivors.

Scope and Then combine on one relation. Both return a RelationLoader, which has Scope and Then methods itself, so a filtered, ordered relation with nested loads is one loader ("approved comments, newest first, each with its author"):

err := momo.LoadAll(ctx, db, documents,
    document.Comments.Scope(
        momo.LoadWhere[models.Comment](comment.Approved.Eq(true)),
        momo.LoadOrderBy[models.Comment](comment.ID.Desc()),
    ).Then(comment.Author),
)
  • API note: Relation.Scope and Relation.Then used to return Loader[P] and now return RelationLoader[P, C], which implements Loader[P]. Passing them to Load, LoadAll, Preload or Then, or assigning them to a Loader[P], compiles unchanged. Only code that declares a variable with the inferred type and then assigns a different loader to it needs a var l momo.Loader[P] declaration.
  • Scope(...).Then(...) and Then(...).Scope(...) are the same loader. Calling either more than once accumulates: predicates AND together, order items append, a later LoadPerParentLimit replaces an earlier one, nested loaders append. A RelationLoader is a value, so a base loader can be shared.
  • The options apply to this relation's children only. Nested loaders carry their own options, so author.Documents.Then(document.Comments.Scope(...)) scopes the comments, not the documents.
  • The nested level runs once over exactly the children that survived the options, so the statement count stays one per bind-limit chunk at the top and one per level below it. A child excluded by LoadWhere is never a nested parent.
  • With no options and no nested loaders a RelationLoader behaves like the plain relation. An error or cancelled context at the nested level is returned from LoadAll.

docs.title: Chunking
docs.text:
Parent keys are sent as bind parameters, and every dialect caps how many a statement may carry. Momo splits the parent keys into chunks that fit under the dialect's limit and runs one statement per chunk, so a load of any size works. WithMaxParams(n) lowers the limit for a DB. Use it for tests that want to exercise chunking with small data, or for databases configured below the dialect's default:

db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithMaxParams(100))

If a scope alone binds so many arguments that no key fits under the limit, the load fails with ErrValidation before any statement runs.

docs.title: Counting children for many parents
docs.text:
Relation.Count counts one parent per statement. To show a count next to each row of a list, LoadCounts counts all parents at once: one grouped SELECT key, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY key per bind-limit chunk.

counts, err := momo.LoadCounts(ctx, db, docs, document.Comments,
    momo.LoadWhere[models.Comment](comment.Approved.Eq(true)))
// counts[i] is the number of approved comments of docs[i]
  • The result has one entry per parent, in parent order. A parent with no children or a NULL key counts zero; parents sharing a key share the count.
  • Has-one, has-many (including polymorphic) and many-to-many relations are supported, with composite keys. Belongs-to fails with ErrUnsupported, as Count does.
  • The load options that narrow the children apply: LoadWhere, and the soft-delete default with LoadWithDeleted and LoadOnlyDeleted. LoadOrderBy is ignored; LoadPerParentLimit fails with ErrValidation.
  • Many-to-many counts join-table rows, like Count. The far table is joined when it has a soft-delete column and LoadWithDeleted is not set, or when a LoadWhere filter applies. Otherwise nothing is joined, so join rows whose far row no longer exists (dangling rows) are counted too.
  • Parent keys are chunked under the dialect bind limit (see Chunking), and a relation hook sees one event per call.

To order or filter parents by their child count inside a query, use CountOrder (section 5).

docs.title: 3. Preload and single-query loading
docs.text:
SelectQuery.Preload attaches loaders to a query. All, One and First run them after the rows are read, with the same statements LoadAll would use. Preload returns a copy, so a base query can be reused, and a query with no result rows runs no relation statement. Inside a transaction the loads run in that transaction.

docs, err := momo.Select[models.Document](db).
    Preload(document.Author, document.Comments.Scope(
        momo.LoadPerParentLimit[models.Comment](3))).
    Limit(20).
    All(ctx)

Each and Iter stream rows without collecting them, so they cannot batch relation loads. With preloads they return ErrUnsupported.

docs.title: Joined
docs.text:
Relation.Joined() folds a belongs-to relation into the parent statement as a LEFT JOIN, so it costs no extra round trip. Pass it to Preload. It does not work with Load, LoadAll, Scope or Then. A matched joined child with NULL in a column its Go field cannot hold fails with ErrValidation and an error naming the child column (column=...).

docs, err := momo.Select[models.Document](db).
    Preload(document.Author.Joined(), document.Comments).
    Limit(20).
    All(ctx)

Here Author arrives with the document rows, and Comments is still loaded with a second statement. Restrictions:

  • To-one belongs-to only, and only when the relation's child key is the child's primary key or a single unique column. That is what guarantees the join cannot multiply parent rows, so Limit, Offset, OrderBy and Where of the parent query keep their meaning. Has-one, has-many and many-to-many fail with ErrUnsupported when the query runs.
  • Not with GroupBy, Having or row locking on the same query (FOR UPDATE cannot lock the nullable side of an outer join), and not with Each or Iter. All of these return ErrUnsupported.
  • If the query sets its own select list with Columns, it must have one expression per mapped field, or the query fails with ErrValidation.
  • The parent's columns are qualified by the parent table in the select list, so a raw, unqualified column name in the parent's Where can become ambiguous with the joined table's columns. Qualify raw column names.
  • Semantics match Load for belongs-to: a NULL foreign key, or a key that matches no child, leaves the field nil (never a zero struct), soft-deleted children are excluded by a condition in the ON clause so the parent row survives, and each parent gets its own copy of a shared child.
  • A joined load runs no statement of its own, so it emits no RelationEvent. The parent statement is reported to the query hook as usual.

docs.title: 4. Pipelined loading
docs.text:
LoadAll (and so Load and Preload) works in levels: the top level holds the relations you listed, and each Then adds a level. On a connection whose driver implements Batcher, which the pgx driver does on the pool, on a transaction and on a pinned connection, all statements of a level, including every bind-limit chunk, are sent in one round trip. Other drivers (the database/sql adapters, SQLite, MySQL) load sequentially. The result is the same either way. There is nothing to enable and no per-call opt-out.

Two differences to know about:

  • Memory. A pipelined level buffers all of its child rows before assigning any, so peak memory is roughly twice that of sequential loading, which holds one relation's rows at a time. Large child sets with a per-parent limit or a LoadWhere stay cheap; an unscoped load of a huge has-many does not.
  • Hook event order. Sequential loading interleaves each relation's events with its statements. A pipelined level reports BeforeRelation for every relation, then BeforeQuery for every statement and one round trip, then AfterQuery per statement as result sets are read, then nested loads, assignment and AfterRelation per relation. The batch runs under the context of the first statement's hooks, so cancelling that context stops the whole batch, and a statement's AfterQuery duration includes its wait for the batch.

A batch is all or nothing: if one statement fails, every relation's AfterRelation reports the error and the parents keep the empty associations. If the driver rejects the batch before sending anything (ErrUnsupported with Op "batch"), Momo falls back to sequential loading for that level.

docs.title: 5. Relation predicates and traversal
docs.text:
Relations also filter and order queries without loading anything.

// Documents with at least one approved comment.
withApproved := momo.Select[models.Document](db).
    Where(document.Comments.Has(comment.Approved.As("momo_r").Eq(true)))

// Documents without any comments.
quiet := momo.Select[models.Document](db).Where(document.Comments.HasNo())

// Documents ordered by number of comments, most-commented first.
busy := momo.Select[models.Document](db).
    OrderBy(document.Comments.CountOrder(momo.DirDesc), document.ID.Asc())
  • Has(scope...) renders EXISTS (...) over the child table, correlated with the parent through the relation's key columns. It is always a subquery, never a join, so it cannot duplicate parent rows.
  • HasNo(scope...) renders NOT EXISTS.
  • HasFrom(parentAlias, scope...) is Has with an explicit parent alias. Self-referencing relations need it: when the outer query aliases the parent table, pass that alias so the subquery correlates with the right instance.
  • CountOrder(dir) orders parents by their number of children, using a correlated COUNT(*). dir is momo.DirAsc or momo.DirDesc.
  • Soft-deleted children do not count. For many-to-many relations the join table gets no soft-delete filter: only the child table's marker applies.

Scope predicates must name the child through the alias momo_r, because the subquery owns that alias. Build them with As on the generated column: comment.Approved.As("momo_r").Eq(true). A predicate that uses the column without the alias refers to the outer query's table.

Relation.From(parents) goes the other way: it returns a SelectQuery[C] of the children whose key is in the key set of the given parent query. The parent query is embedded as a subquery, so no parent row is fetched:

comments := document.Comments.From(
    momo.Select[models.Document](db).Where(document.ID.Eq(int64(1))))
rows, err := comments.All(ctx)

From does not support many-to-many relations. The returned query fails with ErrValidation when it runs.

docs.title: 6. Association helpers
docs.text:
Link, Unlink, Replace and Count write and count the link itself, with no model in between:

doc := models.Document{ID: 1}
tags := []*models.Tag{{ID: 1}, {ID: 2}}

err := document.Tags.Link(ctx, db, &doc, tags...)    // add pairs
err = document.Tags.Unlink(ctx, db, &doc, tags[0])   // remove one pair
err = document.Tags.Replace(ctx, db, &doc, tags[1])  // make this the whole set
n, err := document.Tags.Count(ctx, db, &doc)         // how many are linked

They only need the keys of the parent and children. They never modify the values you pass in.

They write SQL directly. Model hooks, field hooks and an UpdatedAt column are not touched. Use the model's own update path when those must run.

Statement contract, per relation kind (one statement per chunk; a small call is one statement):

Call Has-one, has-many Many-to-many Link UPDATE child SET fk = ? WHERE pk IN (...); a polymorphic relation also sets the discriminator INSERT into the join table that skips existing pairs (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; MySQL ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE with a no-op); relies on a primary or unique key over the join columns Unlink UPDATE child SET fk = NULL WHERE fk = ? AND pk IN (...); a polymorphic relation also adds the discriminator predicate DELETE FROM join WHERE parent cols = ? AND (child cols) IN (...) Replace diff, then unlink the removed and link the added same Count SELECT COUNT(*) over the children counts join rows, joined to the far table when it has a soft-delete column

What this means in practice:

  • Join tables need a unique key. Many-to-many Link relies on a primary or unique key over the join columns to detect an existing pair. Join tables generated from many2many tags already have a composite primary key over the two columns, plus two foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE. A hand-written join table needs a primary or unique key too, or Link inserts duplicate rows.
  • Has-one and has-many Unlink and Replace need a nullable foreign key, because they clear it. On a NOT NULL column they fail with ErrNotNullViolation, with a message saying so. Delete the children instead if they cannot exist without a parent. For the same reason they cannot be used when the child's foreign key column is part of its primary key (for example exams keyed by license_id, exam_id): the database rejects the NULL. Delete those children instead.
  • Replace is a transaction. On a *DB it opens one, on a *Tx it runs in a savepoint. With no children it clears the set in one statement. Otherwise it reads the current child keys, diffs them in Go against the requested set, unlinks only the removed keys and links only the added ones, in chunks, so kept children are not rewritten and a set of any size works.
  • Replace locks the parent row (SELECT 1 ... FOR UPDATE) on PostgreSQL and MySQL, so concurrent Replace calls on the same parent run one after the other. SQLite serialises writers and skips the lock. The lock is a row lock: a parent that does not exist locks nothing. On a *Tx the lock is held until the caller's transaction ends. Link and Unlink take no parent lock and can interleave with a concurrent Replace.
  • Belongs-to is not linkable. Every helper returns ErrUnsupported. Set the foreign key on the parent and update it.
  • Link, Unlink and Replace return ErrValidation when the parent key is NULL, or, for many-to-many, when a child key is NULL. Link and Unlink with no children are no-ops that issue no statement. Count of a parent with a NULL key is zero.
  • Chunks and transactions. When Link or Unlink needs more than one chunk and the Querier is a *DB, the chunks run in one transaction, so the call is atomic. On a *Tx they run in your transaction without a savepoint. If a later chunk fails, the earlier chunks stay applied until you roll back. Chunk size follows the dialect bind limit, see WithMaxParams.

docs.title: 7. Graph writes
docs.text: Graph writes are explicit. Nothing saves a relation you did not name.

docs.title: CreateGraph
docs.text:
CreateGraph inserts a parent and the children of the relations you list, in one transaction. List relations with Relation.Include():

doc := models.Document{
    Title:    "Hello",
    Author:   &models.Author{Name: "Ada"},
    Comments: []models.Comment{{Body: "first"}, {Body: "second"}},
}
err := momo.CreateGraph(ctx, db, &doc,
    document.Author.Include(),
    document.Comments.Include(),
)
  • Listed belongs-to children are inserted first and their key is copied into the parent. Listed has-one and has-many children are inserted after the parent, with the parent's key (read back with RETURNING when it is generated) copied into each child, and the discriminator set for a polymorphic relation. Many-to-many children are inserted and then linked through the join table. Relations are processed in the order listed.
  • The graph is one level deep. Children's own relations are not followed, so a self-referencing relation or an in-memory cycle cannot recurse. A model that appears as its own child fails with ErrValidation.
  • Every row goes through the ordinary insert path, so field hooks, automatic timestamps, Go-side defaults and validation run as for a plain Insert.
  • Many-to-many children are always inserted, not looked up. A child that is already stored is inserted again and fails with ErrUniqueViolation, which undoes the whole graph. Link existing rows with Link instead.
  • Has-many and many-to-many children are inserted with the chunked bulk insert: one multi-row statement per bind-limit chunk, so 1000 children cost one statement, not 1000. A has-one or belongs-to child is a single insert.
  • The bulk insert's RETURNING rows are matched to the children in insertion order. If the database returns fewer or more rows than were inserted (a BEFORE INSERT trigger that skips a row, say), the graph fails with ErrValidation and is undone instead of leaving children without keys.
  • A dialect without RETURNING (MySQL) returns ErrUnsupported before a transaction is opened.
  • On a *DB the graph runs in a new transaction. On a *Tx it runs in a savepoint, so a failure undoes the whole graph and leaves your transaction usable. A dialect without savepoints returns ErrUnsupported there.

docs.title: FindOrCreate
docs.text:
a := models.Author{Name: "Ada"}
created, err := momo.FindOrCreate(ctx, db, []momo.ColumnRef{author.Name}, &a)

FindOrCreate inserts the model unless a row with the same key columns exists. Afterwards the model holds the stored row, and created says whether this call inserted it.

  • The key columns need a unique constraint. The statement is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING, so the constraint decides the winner and concurrent callers never create duplicates; the losers re-select the winner's row. Without a constraint on exactly those columns the database rejects the statement. Dialects without ON CONFLICT or RETURNING return ErrUnsupported before any statement runs.
  • When the row exists, all mapped columns of the model are overwritten by the stored values, and its relation fields are reset.
  • A soft-deleted row is not "found". FindOrCreate never returns or restores a row you deleted, and it does not create a second row with the same key: the unique constraint still holds the soft-deleted row's key, so the insert conflicts and the call fails with ErrUniqueViolation (the deleted row is left untouched, and your model is not overwritten). This holds when the unique constraint covers soft-deleted rows, the case FindOrCreate supports. A partial unique index (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) would let a new row in, but FindOrCreate cannot target it: its ON CONFLICT (key) has no index predicate, so the database rejects the statement. For keys that soft-deleted rows release, use Insert with OnConflict(key).Where(...) and DoNothing, then re-select. To reuse the old row, restore it first; to create a new one, use a different key. A model without a soft-delete column is unaffected. This is the least surprising choice: returning the deleted row would hand back data the application removed, and restoring it would undo a delete silently.
  • Isolation. Under READ COMMITTED the conflicting insert waits for a concurrent transaction and the re-select then sees its row. Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, the re-select can miss a row committed after the snapshot and return ErrNotFound. Retry the transaction in that case.
  • An empty key, a key column the model does not map, or a nil model returns ErrValidation.

docs.title: UpsertByPK
docs.text:
err := momo.UpsertByPK(ctx, db, &a)

UpsertByPK inserts the model, or updates the row with the same primary key: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col. It is the one-call form of Upsert(q).Model(m). Generated columns are read back into the model. The primary key, version, soft-delete and created-at columns are never overwritten. Use the Upsert builder directly when the conflict target is a different unique key, or when you want to choose which columns update.

docs.title: 8. Observability
docs.text:
A hook registered with WithHook that also implements RelationHook receives one event per relation load:

type relLogger struct{ momo.Hook } // embed a Hook for the query events

func (relLogger) BeforeRelation(ctx context.Context, e *momo.RelationEvent) context.Context {
    return ctx
}

func (relLogger) AfterRelation(ctx context.Context, e *momo.RelationEvent) {
    log.Printf("%s.%s %s: %d parents, %d children, %d queries, %s, err=%v",
        e.Parent, e.Name, e.Kind, e.Parents, e.Children, e.Queries, e.Duration, e.Err)
}

db := momo.New(drv, momo.WithHook(relLogger{queryHook}))

RelationEvent fields:

Field Meaning Parent, Name parent table and relation name Kind belongs-to, has-one, has-many or many-to-many Parents number of parents the load ran for Queries child statements compiled for the load; a failed load may have run fewer Children children loaded; set only when the statements succeeded, zero on error Duration filled before AfterRelation Err the load's error

Events fire only for loads that execute statements. They do not fire when there are no parents, when the load fails while being prepared (validation or unsupported options), or for joined loads. BeforeRelation may return a derived context, which later hooks and the load's statements see. For event order under pipelining, see Pipelined loading.

docs.title: 9. Errors and limitations
docs.text:
Errors are *momo.Error values. Test them with errors.Is(err, momo.ErrX). The Op field names the operation.

Operation Error When Load, LoadAll, Preload ErrValidation negative LoadPerParentLimit; invalid descriptor; scope binds too many arguments for the bind limit ErrUnsupported LoadPerParentLimit on belongs-to or has-one; Each or Iter on a query with preloads ErrTooManyRows has-one matched more than one child for a parent Joined ErrUnsupported not belongs-to, child key not unique, GroupBy, Having, locks, Each, Iter; used with Load, LoadAll, Scope or Then ErrValidation select list does not have one expression per mapped field Has, HasNo, CountOrder none of their own an error in the scope predicate surfaces when the query runs From ErrValidation many-to-many relation Link, Unlink, Replace, Count ErrUnsupported belongs-to ErrValidation Link, Unlink, Replace: NULL parent key, or NULL child key on many-to-many. Count with a NULL parent key returns 0, no error ErrNotNullViolation has-one or has-many Unlink or Replace on a NOT NULL foreign key ErrUniqueViolation has-one Link that would break a unique foreign key on the child ErrTxDone the *Tx passed in is already committed or rolled back CreateGraph ErrValidation nil parent, a model listed as its own child, a NULL key that must be copied ErrUnsupported *Tx on a dialect without savepoints; identity read-back on a dialect without RETURNING FindOrCreate ErrValidation nil model, empty key, unmapped key column ErrNotFound re-select misses the winner's row under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE ErrUniqueViolation the key is held by a soft-deleted row ErrUnsupported dialect without ON CONFLICT or RETURNING UpsertByPK ErrValidation nil model

Database errors (unique, foreign key, check, not-null violations, serialization failures) are classified the same way as for any other statement.

Known limitations and follow-ups:

  • A tag-declared belongs_to needs a single-column primary key on its target (the referencing model's key may be composite); has_one and has_many need one on the parent; many2many needs one on both models. Other composite keys work with hand-written descriptors but cannot be expressed with tags.
  • Joined covers belongs-to only. Has-one is not joinable.
  • Pipelining has no public opt-out and doubles peak memory for a level.
  • Link, Unlink and Replace bypass model and field hooks and UpdatedAt.
  • Replace serialises concurrent callers only when the parent row exists, and Link and Unlink are never serialised against it.
  • CreateGraph is one level deep and always inserts; it does not match existing rows.

docs.title: Read replicas
docs.text: WithReplicas registers read-replica drivers on the primary DB. The primary handle never reads from them. DB.Replica with an index returns a handle whose reads may go to that replica; it returns ErrUnsupported when that replica is not configured, and replicas do not chain.

docs.title: What goes to a replica
docs.text:
A statement goes to the replica only when it is clearly a plain read: one statement that starts with SELECT, WITH, VALUES or TABLE, or with EXPLAIN, its options (ANALYZE, VERBOSE, a parenthesised list) and then one of those. It must contain none of these words outside literals, quoted identifiers and comments: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, INTO, COPY, CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, REFRESH, EXECUTE, CALL, DO, LISTEN, NOTIFY, LOCK, DECLARE, GRANT, REVOKE, VACUUM, ANALYZE, CLUSTER, REINDEX, COMMENT, SECURITY, IMPORT; no row lock clause (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR KEY SHARE); none of the side-effect functions nextval, setval, lastval, set_config, pg_notify, txid_current, pg_terminate_backend, pg_cancel_backend, lo_import, lo_export, lo_unlink, dblink_exec, pg_reload_conf, pg_switch_wal, pg_logical_emit_message, or the advisory-lock functions; and no dollar-quoted body. A semicolon followed by more text (a second statement) is refused. Anything else goes to the primary. The list is wide on purpose: a false positive, for example an unquoted column called comment, only costs a read on the primary.

These never go to a replica, whatever the handle:

  • every write (Exec), and every transaction, including reads inside one;
  • INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE with RETURNING;
  • locking reads, such as FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
  • raw SQL that writes, such as a WITH that contains DML, or a SELECT of nextval.

One case cannot be detected: a SELECT that calls a user-defined function which writes looks like a plain read. Run such a call on the primary handle or inside a transaction. The classifier is covered by TestReplicaRoutesWritesAndLocksToPrimary.

A statement that goes to the primary because it is not a plain read counts as a write of the unit of work, so the reads that follow it in the same context see its effects.

docs.title: Combining with other options
docs.text: DB.Replica returns ErrUnsupported on a DB built with WithImplicitTx: that option runs every statement in its own primary transaction, so a replica could never be used. A read on a replica runs outside any transaction, so WithTxSetup does not apply to it. Do not rely on a setting that WithTxSetup installs, such as a row-level-security tenant, for replica reads; use the primary handle for tenant-scoped reads.

docs.title: Reading your own writes
docs.text: Replicas lag. Pass a context from NewUnitOfWork through one request: the first write made through any handle with that context is recorded, and from then on reads of a Replica handle in that context go to the primary. Wrap a context with AllowStaleReads to send reads back to the replica after a write when stale data is acceptable (TestReadReplicaRouting).

docs.title: When the replica is down
docs.text: If the replica fails with a connection-class error when a read starts (connection refused or reset, EOF, a network error, SQLSTATE class 08, 57P01 to 57P03 or 53300), that read runs on the primary (TestReplicaFailureFallsBackToPrimary). Other errors, such as a syntax error, are returned as they are, and so are errors raised after rows have started to arrive: there is no retry in the middle of a result set. A cancelled or expired caller context is never retried.
