docs.title: Testing applications with momotest
docs.text:
github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momotest gives your tests a real PostgreSQL database, isolated per test, with your project's migrations already applied. It replaces the hand-written scratch-database helper that every application would otherwise copy.

Do not mock momo.DB, momo.Tx or momo.Querier. The query builders are the code under test; the constraints and the SQL are what you want to exercise.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Point the tests at a server you may create schemas on:
export MOMO_TEST_POSTGRES_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/scratch

The value must be a postgres:// or postgresql:// URL. Use a database you do not mind filling with temporary schemas; a disposable container is ideal.

  1. Embed the migrations in the package that owns the schema, so the binary and its tests share them:
//go:embed migrations
var files embed.FS

func Migrations() fs.FS { sub, _ := fs.Sub(files, "migrations"); return sub }
  1. Keep tests that use the kit behind the integration build tag (or one of your own), and run them with -tags integration. A plain go test then never touches a database.

When the variable is unset, the test is skipped. Set MOMO_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 in CI and the test fails instead, so a misconfigured job cannot pass by skipping everything. WithEnv reads a different variable.

docs.title: One database per test: New
docs.text:
func TestSignup(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()
    db := momotest.New(t, momotest.WithMigrations(app.Migrations()))
    // db is a *momo.DB on a schema no other test can see.
}

New creates a schema, applies the migrations to it and returns a *momo.DB. When the test ends the pool is closed and the schema is dropped. Code under test may open and commit its own transactions. Use this mode when it does.

docs.title: A rollback per test: NewTx
docs.text:
func TestOverdraft(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()
    tx := momotest.NewTx(t, momotest.WithMigrations(app.Migrations()))
    // tx is a *momo.Tx; everything written through it is gone after the test.
}

The migrations are applied once to a template schema, named after a hash of the migration files, the extension list and the momo version, and kept on the server between runs. The first NewTx in a test binary builds it (or finds it ready) under an advisory lock, over a short-lived administrator connection; after that success the binary remembers it, and each later test only opens its own small pool and begins a transaction, which is much cheaper than New. A changed migration gets a new template; old momotest_tpl_* schemas can be dropped at any time between runs.

The Tx is adopted: Commit and Rollback on it return an error matching momo.ErrAdoptedTx, so a test cannot make its writes permanent. tx.Tx opens savepoints, so you can test a failing step and keep going. Two limits follow from using one transaction per test:

  • Code that must commit, or that needs two connections to see each other's work, belongs in a test that uses New.
  • Parallel tests do not see each other's rows, but two that insert the same unique key wait for each other until one finishes. Give parallel tests distinct keys.
  • DDL, TRUNCATE and LOCK TABLE inside a NewTx test take locks that block every other parallel test using the same template until this one ends. Run such tests with New.
  • Identity and sequence values are consumed by a rolled-back transaction, so never assert a literal generated id; compare with the id that Insert read back.

docs.title: Migrations must stay in their schema
docs.text:
Migrations run in a schema of the test's own, with public after it on the search path. Write them unqualified. momotest refuses early, with the file name, a migration that contains CREATE SCHEMA, or CREATE EXTENSION for an extension not listed in WithExtensions: an extension exists once per database, so it would land in one test's schema and vanish under the others when that schema is dropped. List extensions in WithExtensions (names are matched in lower case); they are installed once in public.

The check reads the SQL with comments and string literals removed, so a comment that mentions create schema is fine and CREATE /* x */ EXTENSION foo is still caught. Quoted identifiers are kept. Dollar-quoted bodies are checked as code, because a DO block can run CREATE EXTENSION: the cost is that text inside a dollar-quoted string that looks like that statement is also refused, with a message naming the file. Move such text into a normal string, or list the extension.

NewTx remembers the result of the check and the template name per migration fs.FS value and extension list. Build the FS once, in a package variable or an embed.FS, so that the files are walked once; an FS rebuilt on every call (such as fs.Sub inside a function) is re-read each time, which still works. Only successes are remembered, so a failed read fails one test and the next one tries again. Changing the files behind a remembered FS while the test binary runs, for example rewriting the directory an os.DirFS points at, is not supported.

docs.title: Leftover schemas
docs.text: Cleanup runs in t.Cleanup, so a killed test run (kill -9, a CI timeout) can leave momotest_<hex> schemas behind. They are harmless but accumulate. Drop them on a disposable server by recreating it, or with DROP SCHEMA momotest_<hex> CASCADE for each name in pg_namespace that matches momotest\_% and is not momotest_tpl_%. Template schemas momotest_tpl_* are meant to stay. momotest has no sweep helper: it never drops a schema it did not create in the current test.

docs.title: Fixtures: Seed
docs.text:
org := &models.Org{Name: "acme"}
momotest.Seed(t, tx,
    momotest.Insert(org),
    momotest.Insert(&models.User{OrgID: org.ID, Email: "ada@acme.test"}),
)

Seed runs its steps in the order given, so list a table before the tables that reference it. All steps run in one transaction (a savepoint when the querier is a *momo.Tx); if one fails, nothing is kept and the test fails. Insert reads generated columns, such as identity keys, back into the rows you pass, so later steps can use them. Graph inserts a root with the related rows it includes, as momo.CreateGraph does. A step is any func(ctx, momo.Querier) error, so custom fixtures fit too.

docs.title: Fixtures from a file: LoadFixtures
docs.text:
momotest.LoadFixtures(t, q, path) inserts the rows of a YAML file into q, a *momo.DB or a *momo.Tx, for data that is easier to read as a file than as Go structs. The file maps a table name to a list of rows, and each row maps a column name to a value:

authors:
  - id: 1
    name: Ada
documents:
  - id: 1
    author_id: 1
    title: First
  - id: 2
    author_id: null
    title: Orphan

Tables are inserted in file order and the rows of a table in list order, so list a table before the tables that reference it. Columns are written sorted by name and a YAML null becomes SQL NULL. Table and column names are quoted with momo.Ident and every value is a bound argument, so a value is never spliced into the SQL. A table name is one identifier, with no schema prefix. A value is a string, integer, float, bool, null, timestamp or !!binary (read as bytes); a nested map or list is refused. LoadFixtures writes plain INSERT statements and is tested on PostgreSQL and SQLite; it has not been run against MySQL or MariaDB. A file that is not a mapping of tables to lists of rows, a missing file, and a row the database refuses (a foreign key to a row that is not there, say) fail the test with a message that names the file, the table and the row. Each row is its own statement, so rows before a failing one stay unless you pass a transaction.

docs.title: SQLite without a server: sqlitetest
docs.text:
github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momotest/sqlitetest gives a test a SQLite database with sqlite-vec loaded, without a server and without an environment variable: sqlitetest.New(t, opts...) returns a *momo.DB on a new file in the test's own temporary directory. Every call opens a file of its own, so two databases in one test never see each other's tables and parallel tests do not collide. The database is closed and the file removed when the test ends. The options go to momo.New, for example momo.WithHook, and LoadFixtures fills it like any other database. The database starts empty: create the tables with your own DDL, for example momo.SQLiteVectorType for a vector column (see Vector search); momotest.WithMigrations and NewTx are PostgreSQL features and do not apply.

SQLite lives in its own package, and not in momotest, because the SQLite driver is compiled from C sources: a test binary that imports only momotest for PostgreSQL does not build them, and a repository test (TestMomotestAvoidsSQLite) keeps it that way. Only a test that imports sqlitetest pays for them. The driver needs cgo and a non-Windows target; on any other build sqlitetest.New skips the test, the way momotest.New skips when the server URL is unset.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Effect WithMigrations(fs.FS) Apply these migrations. The directory needs no momo.sum. Without it the database is empty. WithEnv(name) Read the server URL from another variable. WithExtensions(names) CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS in public first; with vector the pool registers the codec. WithMomoOptions(opts) Passed to momo.New, for example a hook. WithMaxConns(n) Pool size per test: 4 for New, 2 for NewTx by default.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: Every call opens its own connection pool and, in New, its own schema, so t.Parallel and -race are safe. The one shared step, creating extensions and building a template, runs under a PostgreSQL advisory lock (keyed by hashtext of the names momotest:extensions and momotest:template), so tests in one binary and several test binaries running at once (go test ./...) cooperate. New also opens a short administrator connection to create and, at cleanup, drop its schema. A NewTx test holds one connection for its transaction, plus the pool's spare. Each parallel test holds a few connections; keep the server's max_connections above the number of parallel tests times the pool size, or lower the pool with WithMaxConns or the parallelism with -parallel.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: examples/testing runs a small bank-account service through both modes, in parallel, with seeded fixtures. Its test is the reference for how to write yours.

docs.title: Vector search
docs.text: Momo supports pgvector on PostgreSQL: value types, typed distance expressions, HNSW and IVFFlat index declarations, scoped search settings, plan inspection and an opt-in binary wire codec. It also runs the float32 and bit vector builders on SQLite with sqlite-vec, and the distance builders on MariaDB. This page describes what is built. Every Go snippet below is an Example function in example_vector_test.go (package momo) or vector/example_test.go (package vector), so go test compiles it and checks its printed output.

docs.title: Platforms and versions
docs.text:
• SQLite with sqlite-vec v0.1.6, through driver/sqlitedriver (cgo, not Windows); see SQLite and sqlite-vec below.
  • PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension. Integration tests run against pgvector 0.8.7 (pgvector/pgvector:0.8.7-pg17 primary, 0.8.7-pg16 for an older major). The iterative scan settings need pgvector 0.8.0 or newer.
  • The vector extension must be installed by a role that may create it. Momo never installs it at connect time. A missing extension surfaces as momo.ErrUnsupported from a migration, with the extension named in the message. A search settings call checks the installed version the same way.

docs.title: Not yet available
docs.text:
These parts of the vector plan are not built on this branch, so there is no API to document yet:

  • Hybrid search: PostgreSQL full-text plus vector search fused by reciprocal rank (planned options TextCandidates, VectorCandidates and RRFK, with k=60 as the default) does not exist yet.
  • MySQL and MariaDB: see "MariaDB and MySQL" below. The migration engine for MySQL does not exist yet, so no tool creates VECTOR columns or indexes.

docs.title: Value types
docs.text:
The vector package holds the four Go types. Each has a Validate(dim) method, a Value method that produces the pgvector text form and a Scan method that reads it back. Validation errors wrap vector.ErrInvalidVector, which the root package re-exports as momo.ErrInvalidVector.

Go type PostgreSQL type Notes vector.Vector vector(n) float32, dimension 1 to 16000 (vector.MaxDim) vector.HalfVector halfvec(n) float32 in Go, float16 in storage, each value within 65504 vector.SparseVector sparsevec(n) Dim, zero-based strictly increasing Indices, Values vector.Bits bit(n) Len bits packed most significant bit first, trailing bits 0

Value rules, enforced before a value reaches the server:

  • The length must equal the column dimension declared on the VectorColumn, unless the column is dimensionless (see Dimensionless columns).
  • NaN and Inf are rejected.
  • A halfvec component must satisfy |x| <= 65504.
  • A dimension above 16000 is rejected for vector and halfvec.
  • A sparsevec has at most 16000 stored elements (vector.MaxSparseNNZ) and a dimension up to 1,000,000,000 (vector.MaxSparseDim). Its text form uses one-based indices, as pgvector does, while Indices is zero-based.
  • A bit string has at most vector.MaxBits bits, the PostgreSQL limit.

The Example functions ExampleVector, ExampleHalfVector, ExampleSparseVector and ExampleBits in vector/example_test.go show the validation and the text forms:

v := vector.Vector{1, 2.5, -3}
fmt.Println(v.Validate(3))      // <nil>
text, _ := v.Value()
fmt.Println(text)               // [1,2.5,-3]
errors.Is(v.Validate(4), vector.ErrInvalidVector) // true

docs.title: Columns and distances
docs.text:
A momo.VectorColumn[V] is a typed column descriptor that carries the declared dimension. Generated code emits one for every field of a vector package type, with the dimension from the dim tag, so document.Embedding passes straight to a distance builder. Build one by hand with momo.NewVectorColumn only for a table the generator does not cover.

A vector column offers the predicates, ordering and write methods of a plain column (Eq, In, IsNull, IsNotNull, IsDistinctFrom, Asc, Desc, Set, SetExpr, SetDefault, SetExcluded), except the range comparisons Lt, Le, Gt, Ge and Between: vectors have no meaningful total order, so use a distance builder to order them. A nullable field (*vector.Vector) gets momo.NullVectorColumn, which adds SetNull.

A vector field tagged read_only, create_only or immutable gets the matching ReadOnlyVectorColumn, CreateOnlyVectorColumn or ImmutableVectorColumn. They keep the write restriction of the plain permission columns (no Set on a read-only column, an insert-only Set on the other two) and every distance builder accepts them, so a read-only embedding can be searched.

The distance builders take a column and a query vector of the same type. Each returns a DistanceExpr, an Expression[float64] that works in the select list, in comparisons and in OrderBy. Asc() orders nearest first and is the default; Desc() orders farthest first.

Builder pgvector operator Column types SQLite function L2Distance <-> vector, halfvec, sparse vec_distance_l2 InnerProductDistance <#> vector, halfvec, sparse none CosineDistance <=> vector, halfvec, sparse vec_distance_cosine L1Distance <+> vector, halfvec, sparse vec_distance_l1 HammingDistance <~> bit vec_distance_hamming JaccardDistance <%> bit none

InnerProductDistance is pgvector's <#>, which returns the negative inner product so that ascending order means closest. Passing a dense vector to a bit builder, or the reverse, does not compile (testdata/compilefail).

The query vector is a bound argument. A dimension mismatch (except on a dimensionless column, see Dimensionless columns), NaN or an out-of-range value is a build error wrapping ErrValidation, reported by SQL() or by the first execution, never a server error. A metric the dialect lacks is a build error wrapping ErrUnsupported. The metrics per dialect come from dialect.Dialect.Vector:

for _, name := range []dialect.Name{dialect.Postgres, dialect.SQLite} {
    caps := dialect.For(name).Vector
    fmt.Println(name, caps.Metrics, caps.Indexes)
}
// postgres [l2 ip cosine l1 hamming jaccard] [hnsw ivfflat]
// sqlite [l2 l1 cosine hamming] []

A nearest-neighbour query (ExampleCosineDistance):

c, err := momo.Select[example.Document](db).
    OrderBy(momo.CosineDistance(document.Embedding, query).Asc()).
    Limit(5).
    SQL()
// ... ORDER BY ("documents"."embedding" <=> $1) ASC LIMIT $2

Reading the distance next to a column subset needs a projection struct (momo.Projection, From and Columns; see projections). A projection read From a table with a soft-delete column gets the same automatic filter as a model, so soft-deleted rows stay out of the results. Add the predicate yourself only when From is a subquery or a hand-built TableRef.

docs.title: Declaring vector columns and indexes
docs.text:
The generator maps vector.Vector, vector.HalfVector, vector.SparseVector and vector.Bits fields to vector, halfvec, sparsevec and bit columns. The dim tag sets the dimension, and sparsevec and bit require it:

Embedding vector.Vector `momo:"dim:1536"`

Generation adds CREATE EXTENSION vector to the schema when a vector column or index is present. An ANN index needs an operator class, and pgvector's hnsw has no default one, so declare vector indexes in MomoConfig (the reference model is internal/testmodels/example/models.go):

func (d *Document) MomoConfig(c *momo.Config) {
    c.Index("documents_embedding_hnsw", &d.Embedding).
        Method("hnsw").
        Opclass(&d.Embedding, "vector_cosine_ops").
        With("m", "16").
        With("ef_construction", "64")
}

The generator and schema.ValidateVectorIndex reject an index that pgvector would refuse, before any SQL runs. The error wraps schema.ErrInvalidVectorIndex. schema.VectorIndexOpClass(type, metric) returns the opclass for a column type and metric (ExampleValidateVectorIndex).

docs.title: Index limits
docs.text:
Method Types Dimension limit Opclasses (suffix after <type>_) hnsw vector, halfvec, sparsevec, bit vector 2000, halfvec 4000, bit 64000 l2, ip, cosine, l1; bit: hamming, jaccard ivfflat vector, halfvec, bit vector 2000, halfvec 4000, bit 64000 l2, ip, cosine; bit: hamming
  • ivfflat does not support sparsevec.
  • hnsw accepts the storage parameters m (2 to 100, default 16) and ef_construction (4 to 1000, default 64, at least 2*m).
  • ivfflat requires an explicit lists parameter (1 to 32768). Momo does not rely on the server default of 100.
  • An index covers one plain column. Expression parts are rejected.
  • Vector indexes exist only on PostgreSQL. Another dialect gets an error.

docs.title: Dimensionless columns
docs.text:
A vector.Vector or vector.HalfVector field without a dim tag maps to the bare vector or halfvec type. Use it for a store whose embedding size depends on the configured model: each row carries its size in a dims column, and every search filters on it.

type KbChunk struct {
    momo.Model `momo:"table:kb_chunks"`
    ID         int64         `momo:"pk,identity"`
    Dims       int
    Embedding  vector.Vector // no dim: any size
}
  • Generation emits a plain vector column and a momo.VectorColumn whose Dim() is zero. sparsevec and bit still require dim.
  • A distance argument of any size is accepted; it is checked against its own size, so NaN, Inf and an empty vector are still rejected. The column never catches a size mismatch itself.
  • pgvector fails a distance between two sizes, so filter on dims in the same query: Where(chunk.Dims.Eq(len(q))) plus OrderBy(momo.CosineDistance(chunk.Embedding, q).Asc()).
  • The migration round-trips the bare type and the next diff is empty.
  • Limit: pgvector cannot build an hnsw or ivfflat index on a dimensionless column. Momo refuses one, with an error that wraps schema.ErrInvalidVectorIndex and names the column. Searches run as a sequential scan over the filtered rows. An expression or partial index such as ((embedding::vector(1536))) WHERE dims = 1536 is not supported yet: expression parts are rejected.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
migrate.Diff emits the extension, the table and the index, and migrate/postgres renders them (Example_vectorMigration):

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "vector"
CREATE TABLE "documents" ("id" bigint NOT NULL, "embedding" vector(3) NOT NULL, ...)
CREATE INDEX "documents_embedding_hnsw" ON "documents" USING "hnsw" ("embedding" "vector_cosine_ops") WITH ("m" = 16, "ef_construction" = 64)

Inspection reads method, operator class and storage parameters back, so an unchanged vector index produces no diff. A default operator class (ivfflat on vector, vector_l2_ops) is stored as empty, which matches inspection.

docs.title: Search settings
docs.text:
momo.SearchSettings applies pgvector settings for one transaction. Zero values leave the server default alone. Settings use set_config(name, value, true), so they revert at commit or rollback and never reach a pooled connection, which makes them safe behind PgBouncer in transaction mode.

Field Setting Range HNSWEfSearch hnsw.ef_search 1 to 1000 HNSWIterativeScan hnsw.iterative_scan IterativeOff, IterativeRelaxedOrder, IterativeStrictOrder HNSWMaxScanTuples hnsw.max_scan_tuples 1 to 2147483647 (server default 20000) HNSWScanMemMultiplier hnsw.scan_mem_multiplier 1 to 1000, float, a multiple of work_mem IVFFlatProbes ivfflat.probes 1 to 32768 IVFFlatIterativeScan ivfflat.iterative_scan IterativeOff or IterativeRelaxedOrder IVFFlatMaxProbes ivfflat.max_probes 1 to 32768 ExactSearch enable_indexscan, enable_bitmapscan set to off bool

SearchSettings.Validate reports a value outside its range as ErrValidation. The iterative fields, HNSWMaxScanTuples, HNSWScanMemMultiplier and IVFFlatMaxProbes need pgvector 0.8.0 or newer. When any of them is set, SetSearch reads pg_extension and returns ErrUnsupported on an older or missing extension, instead of letting the server accept an unknown setting as a placeholder.

Use DB.WithSearch for a block, or Tx.SetSearch inside a transaction you already have (ExampleDB_WithSearch, ExampleTx_SetSearch):

settings := momo.SearchSettings{
    HNSWEfSearch:      100,
    HNSWIterativeScan: momo.IterativeRelaxedOrder, // needs pgvector 0.8
    HNSWMaxScanTuples: 20000,
    HNSWScanMemMultiplier: 2, // pgvector 0.8: iterative scan memory, times work_mem
}
err := db.WithSearch(ctx, settings, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {
    _, err := momo.Select[example.Document](tx).
        OrderBy(momo.CosineDistance(document.Embedding, query).Asc()).
        Limit(10).
        All(ctx)
    return err
})

Tx.SetLocal(ctx, name, value) sets any run-time parameter the same way. Never pass an untrusted name: the name is bound, but set_config can change role or search_path.

docs.title: Exact versus approximate search
docs.text: An index scan is approximate. ExactSearch turns off index and bitmap scans for the rest of the transaction, so a vector ORDER BY scans the table and returns the exact nearest neighbours. The switches are not specific to vector indexes: every other index lookup in that transaction also falls back to a sequential scan, so keep the transaction short and dedicated to the exact query.

docs.title: Filters, iterative scans and result counts
docs.text:
With a selective filter and LIMIT k, pgvector with iterative scan off scans the index once and applies the filter afterwards, so it can return fewer than k rows. TestFilteredANNIterativeScan reproduces this: a filter that matches 1% of 20000 rows returns fewer than 10 rows with iterative scan off, and 10 with relaxed_order and HNSWMaxScanTuples 20000.

relaxed_order keeps scanning until enough rows pass the filter or hnsw.max_scan_tuples is reached. The result is therefore still approximate, and it can be shorter than k when the filter matches fewer rows than that bound allows. strict_order (hnsw only) keeps exact distance order while it scans.

docs.title: Verifying index use
docs.text:
SelectQuery.Explain(ctx) runs EXPLAIN (never EXPLAIN ANALYZE), binds the parameters and returns the plan text. It does not execute the query. Run it inside the transaction whose settings you want to see (ExampleSelectQuery_Explain):

plan, err := momo.Select[example.Document](db).
    OrderBy(momo.L2Distance(document.Embedding, query).Asc()).
    Limit(10).
    Explain(ctx)
// look for "Index Scan using documents_embedding_hnsw"

TestVectorIndexUsed and TestExactSearchBypassesVectorIndex use this pattern to assert that the index is used, and that ExactSearch stops using it. Expect a sequential scan on a small table, because the planner prefers it below a few thousand rows. Explain returns ErrUnsupported on MySQL.

docs.title: PostgreSQL wire format
docs.text:
By default vector values travel as text. The binary codec is opt-in and lives in driver/pgxdriver:

  • pgxdriver.ConfigureVectors(cfg) installs an AfterConnect hook that looks up the OIDs of vector, halfvec and sparsevec and registers codecs for them and for bit. Call it before pgxpool.NewWithConfig. The lookup runs once per connection: a connection opened before CREATE EXTENSION vector stays on text until the pool recycles it.
  • pgxdriver.WithVectorFormat(pgxdriver.VectorBinary) asks for binary parameters. It needs a describe-based exec mode (WithExecMode with pgx.QueryExecModeDescribeExec, CacheStatement or CacheDescribe); pgx's default QueryExecModeExec always sends text, with identical results.
  • COPY always uses binary and so needs ConfigureVectors.
  • Decoders bound every length they read before they allocate.

ExampleConfigureVectors shows the setup:

cfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig("postgres://localhost/app")
pgxdriver.ConfigureVectors(cfg)
pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, cfg)
db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool, pgxdriver.WithVectorFormat(pgxdriver.VectorBinary)))

docs.title: Differences between approaches
docs.text:
• pgvector exact search (ExactSearch) reads every row and returns the true nearest neighbours. Index search (hnsw, ivfflat) is approximate and tuned with hnsw.ef_search, ivfflat.probes and the iterative settings.
  • sqlite-vec is brute-force KNN with no ANN index. A request for an ANN index on SQLite is ErrUnsupported. SQLite supports float32 vectors (l2, l1, cosine) and bit vectors (hamming) only; halfvec and sparsevec arguments, inner product and Jaccard return ErrUnsupported at build time. SQLite bit vectors keep only the packed bytes, so the declared column length is authoritative for Len. See SQLite and sqlite-vec.
  • SetSearch on SQLite: ExactSearch alone is a no-op, every search is already exact, and any other field is ErrUnsupported.
  • MariaDB VECTOR INDEX is approximate; see "MariaDB and MySQL" below.

docs.title: SQLite and sqlite-vec
docs.text:
driver/sqlitedriver links sqlite-vec v0.1.6 (the version vec_version() reports; sqlitedriver.SQLiteVecVersion is the release it is tested with, and Open fails with ErrUnsupported on another minor or major version but accepts a later patch release such as v0.1.7). The same typed builders that serve pgvector render sqlite-vec's scalar functions, and the integration tests run them against a real SQLite database: vector_sqlite_integration_test.go in the root package and TestSQLiteVectorParity in driver/sqlitedriver. It needs cgo and does not build on Windows. The SQLite migration dialect (migrate/sqlite) is library only, and the generator refuses vector fields on SQLite, so you create the table with your own DDL.

Columns. A vector is a plain BLOB column; sqlite-vec has no declared dimension, so the length is guarded by a CHECK. momo.SQLiteVectorType and momo.SQLiteBitsType return the definition to put after the column name: BLOB CHECK (length("emb") = 12) for three float32 elements and BLOB CHECK (length("bits") = 1) for eight bits. A vector of the wrong size is then refused by the database as ErrCheckViolation. A dimensionless column is ErrUnsupported, because there is no length to check.

Values. vector.Vector is stored as a little-endian float32 blob and read back from one, and vector.Bits as its packed bytes (most significant bit first, as in pgvector: bit 0 is the top bit of byte 0). Both are validated before they are bound (NaN, Inf, an empty vector, a bad bit length are ErrInvalidVector), because a blob has no text form that would reject them later. A *vector.Vector or *vector.Bits field is nullable: nil binds NULL. HalfVector and SparseVector have no sqlite-vec type, so binding one, or searching with one, is ErrUnsupported when the query is built. A bit vector read from SQLite has a Len of 8 times its byte count, so the column length is the authority for a length that is not a multiple of 8.

Metrics. These are exactly the functions v0.1.6 registers:

Builder SQLite function Column type L2Distance vec_distance_l2 vector.Vector L1Distance vec_distance_l1 vector.Vector CosineDistance vec_distance_cosine vector.Vector HammingDistance vec_distance_hamming(vec_bit(column), vec_bit(argument)) vector.Bits InnerProductDistance none: ErrUnsupported at build time JaccardDistance none: ErrUnsupported at build time

The query vector is a bound argument. When the column is sensitive, it shows as momo.RedactedArg in hook events, on a query and on an insert, while the database gets the real blob. Distances work in the select list, in a comparison and in OrderBy (Asc nearest first, Desc farthest first). Results are held to the plain-Go reference in internal/vectorparity: the top-10 ids of cosine, L2 and L1 search over 300 vectors equal the reference exactly. The reference is the one pgvector exact search and MariaDB are held to for cosine, and when a PostgreSQL URL is set TestSQLiteVectorParity also loads the same vectors into pgvector and requires the same ids for cosine, L2 and L1.

Indexes. sqlite-vec compares every row, so it has no approximate index and dialect.For(dialect.SQLite).Vector.Indexes is empty, and schema.ValidateVectorIndex rejects an index for SQLite with schema.ErrInvalidVectorIndex. An internal check turns a request for any index method on a dialect that lists none into ErrUnsupported; it becomes public when a SQLite migration dialect needs it. SQLite itself does not parse an index method, so nothing is accepted silently. ExactSearch in SearchSettings is a no-op (every search is exact) and any other setting is ErrUnsupported. The sqlite-vec virtual tables (vec0, which have an index of their own) are not wrapped.

Bring up a throwaway database for your own tests with momotest/sqlitetest.

docs.title: MariaDB and MySQL
docs.text:
MariaDB 11.8 supports float32 vectors through mysqldriver. MySQL 9.x stores them but cannot compare them.

Capability MariaDB 11.8 MySQL 9.7 MySQL 8.4 Column type VECTOR(N) VECTOR(N) none: ErrUnsupported vector.Vector write and read yes yes no L2Distance VEC_DISTANCE_EUCLIDEAN(col, VEC_FromText(?)) ErrUnsupported ErrUnsupported CosineDistance VEC_DISTANCE_COSINE(col, VEC_FromText(?)) ErrUnsupported ErrUnsupported Other metrics, other types ErrUnsupported (inner product, L1, halfvec, sparsevec, bit) ErrUnsupported ErrUnsupported ANN index VECTOR INDEX, approximate none none Capabilities().Vectors true false false

MySQL Community has no distance function (the distance functions belong to HeatWave), so a distance query on MySQL fails at build time with ErrUnsupported. Momo never falls back to a scan or to a Go-side sort.

A vector.Vector bound on MySQL or MariaDB travels as its text form wrapped in VEC_FromText (MariaDB) or STRING_TO_VECTOR (MySQL), on every typed bind path: insert, update, equality and distance. Stored vectors scan back from the server's binary float32 form. A column marked sensitive masks the vector in hook events exactly as on PostgreSQL.

A MariaDB VECTOR INDEX needs a NOT NULL vector(N) column and accepts M from 3 to 200 and DISTANCE of euclidean or cosine. It serves only the metric it was built with, and an ORDER BY distance with LIMIT uses it. To get the exact nearest neighbours from the same table, add + 0 to the distance in a raw query, which keeps the server from using the index. schema.ValidateMariaDBVectorIndex checks a declaration and schema.MariaDBVectorIndexClause renders it. momo.MySQLVectorType gives the column type for a server version and refuses MySQL 8.4 and MariaDB before 11.7 with a diagnostic that names the version.
